Choosing a method that the budget or time frame cannot support, such as mailing a survey to the whole community.
Describing ethical considerations in general rather than how they apply to this research.

sampleAnswers.answer: Criteria for choosing a research method include the type of data needed, the time and cost available, access to participants, and the ethical issues involved. The student wants to understand reasons, which needs qualitative data, so a questionnaire with mostly closed questions is less suitable. Her budget is $50 and she has four weeks, so a large survey sent to the whole community would be too costly. The most suitable method is a set of semi-structured interviews with about 10 volunteers from the club's list. She would contact the club for permission, explain the purpose and gain written consent from each volunteer, and protect privacy by storing names separately from responses. She would conduct the interviews in person or by phone, record them with consent, and ask the same open questions of each volunteer so the responses can be compared. The sample group would be small, so the findings would describe this club rather than all volunteers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: applies clear criteria from the scenario, rejects a method with reasons, and shows how the chosen method would be carried out ethically. The limitation of the small sample group is a sound closing point.

sampleAnswers.answer: A questionnaire is cheap but gives little reason behind answers, so it is less suitable. The student could interview about ten volunteers from the club, asking open questions, and record their answers with consent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: applies some criteria to reject a questionnaire and chooses interviews with a reasonable justification. Budget, time and privacy are not developed, which limits the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student could interview volunteers to find out their reasons for volunteering.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a method with limited reference to the scenario. No criteria are applied to justify the choice.

dotPoints.description: Research process (planning for research (formulating a research proposal; managing resources, eg time, materials); conducting research (accessing sources of data; collecting and recording data; documenting actions and issues); interpreting research (presenting research findings; analysing research results; drawing conclusions from research))

prompts.question: Why is it important to plan before starting research?
markerNotes: Explain why planning matters to the quality of the research, such as how a timeline keeps the research on track, rather than only saying that planning is good.
Name one or two parts of planning, such as the research proposal, a timeline or choosing sampling methods, and link each to the research outcome.
commonStudentErrors: Saying planning is important without saying what it does for the research.
Describing later stages of the research process, such as collecting or analysing data, instead of planning.
Giving a general point about organisation that could apply to any task rather than to research.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clearly explains in general terms the importance of planning as a part of the research process
2 marks: Provides information about planning for research
1 mark: Provides one relevant point

sampleAnswers.answer:
Planning for research is important as it allows the researcher to formulate a research proposal, which would include creating a timeline which allows the researcher to effectively manage their time and choosing the most suitable types of data to be collected for the chosen topic.
Planning also allows for resources such as time and energy to be managed and selecting appropriate sampling methods to assist in obtaining reliable and valid data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains why planning matters, through the research proposal, timeline and sampling choices, and how these make the data reliable and valid. The answer is short and well matched to 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Planning is important because the researcher needs to know what they are going to do and when. It also helps them manage their time and choose the right data to collect.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: gives information about planning, a timeline and time management, but does not explain why this matters for the research. Saying how a timeline stops the research running late, or how a plan helps the data be valid, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Planning helps the research to be organised.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: one relevant point that planning organises the research, with no development. Explaining why it matters for the data or the timeline would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Apply the research process to a chosen topic by: selecting a research focus; selecting appropriate sampling methods; proposing how the research will be conducted; creating a timeline for research goals; accessing relevant sources of secondary data; using suitable research methods to collect and record primary and secondary data; recording actions and proposing solutions to any research issues; presenting primary data in graphs, tables or written reports; comparing key findings from primary and secondary data; forming research-based conclusions and making recommendations; crediting sources of data by means of bibliography and appendix

prompts.question: Justify steps that would address the research issue presented in the diary.
markerNotes: Identify the issue the diary reveals first, then justify each step by what it fixes; here the target group did not answer under the same conditions, so the results are unreliable.
A justified step says what it fixes and why that makes the research more reliable, such as a set time for everyone and clear instructions.
A step that repeats a problem from the diary without changing it does not address the issue.
commonStudentErrors: Proposing steps without saying why each one addresses the issue in the diary.
Describing the problems in the diary rather than proposing solutions to them.
Suggesting the researcher should do better without a specific change, such as a new time or clearer instructions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Justifies steps to address the research issue presented in the diary
4 marks: Justifies some steps to address the research issue presented in the diary
3 marks: Provides some steps to address the research issue
2 marks: Demonstrates a basic understanding of the issue and/or solutions
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The whole target sample was not able to answer the questionnaire under the same or similar conditions, therefore the research method was unreliable. To solve this issue:
• Set a new time for the whole target group to complete the questionnaire.
• Deliver the instructions for the questionnaire, stating confidentiality to reassure participants.
By setting a new time, a clear process can be followed with enough time to read and answer the questions, give consent, and ensure the process can be repeated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: justifies two steps, a new time and clear instructions with confidentiality, and ties each to the reliability of the research. The answer also explains why a set time lets the process be repeated.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hold the questionnaire again at a set time, and make sure every student has enough time to finish it. Give clear instructions to everyone, and bring enough copies for the whole group so no one is left out.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: provides steps, a set time and 'Give clear instructions to everyone', that address the issue, but gives no justification for either. Explaining why each step makes the results more reliable would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The questionnaire was poorly organised, so the researcher should plan it better.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about the issue, but the step is too general to address it. A specific step, such as a set time, would move it to the 3-mark row.

prompts.scenario:
A diary entry from a student’s Independent Research Project is shown.
Diary entry 3
A questionnaire was created for the IRP hypothesis ‘Artificial intelligence can better prepare school students for future careers’.
- It was organised to hand out a paper questionnaire to our Year 12 cohort during a year meeting.
- We ran out of copies.
- The verbal instructions were unclear, and students were talking.
The disorganisation meant that some students didn’t finish the questionnaire or were really rushed. Also, the hospitality class was on an excursion.
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: All students must study the 2 (two) groups in Category A plus 2 (two) groups selected from Category B

prompts.question: Describe the group selection a student must make to meet the requirements of the course.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Sam is planning his study for the course and wants to know which groups he must cover before he chooses any others.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes both mandatory Category A groups and the two groups selected from Category B, and states that students study four groups in total
3 marks: Describes both mandatory Category A groups and the requirement to select two groups from Category B
2 marks: Identifies the mandatory Category A groups with limited reference to Category B
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the groups studied in the course
markerNotes: Name both Category A groups first, because they are mandatory, then state that two groups are chosen from Category B.
Give the total of four groups and the split of two from each category, so the selection rule is clear.
Naming every Category B group is not required; the marker looks for the rule that two are chosen.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the Category B groups as mandatory and leaving out the Category A groups.
Stating that students choose all their groups, with no mandatory groups.
Listing groups without saying how many must come from each category.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sam must study both Category A groups, which are mandatory: Youth and Rural and remote families. He must also select two groups from Category B, which includes Aged, Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, People with disabilities, LGBTQIA+ communities, Sole parents and Homeless people. Sam therefore studies four groups in total, with two from each category, and he chooses his Category B groups himself. This rule means Sam cannot study only the groups that interest him, because the mandatory groups must be covered first.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: names both mandatory Category A groups, states the two Category B selections and gives the total of four groups. The answer is brief and accurate for 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sam must study Youth and Rural and remote families, and then choose two groups from Category B.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the mandatory Category A groups with a brief reference to Category B. Stating that the Category B choice is two groups would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sam chooses four groups to study in the course.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about the group selection, but neither category is named. Naming the mandatory groups would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess whether Priya’s choice of groups meets the requirements of the course. Refer to both categories of groups in your answer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Priya has chosen four groups for her study: Youth, Aged, Sole parents and Homeless people. She plans to study these four groups and no others.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses Priya’s selection against both category requirements, making a sound judgement of the extent to which it meets the course structure
5 marks: Assesses Priya’s selection against both category requirements, with a clear judgement of its overall success
4 marks: Explains which requirements Priya’s selection meets and does not meet, with some judgement
3 marks: Describes one requirement of the course that Priya’s selection does not meet, with limited judgement
2 marks: Identifies the number of groups Priya has chosen, with limited reference to the requirements
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the groups in the course
markerNotes: Test the selection against each rule separately: the two mandatory Category A groups, then the two Category B groups.
Make a judgement about the extent to which the choice meets the requirements, rather than a yes or no.
Suggest a specific change that would meet the requirements, which shows the assessment has been applied.
commonStudentErrors: Counting the total of four groups as meeting the requirements without checking the split between the categories.
Stating that the choice is wrong without naming which requirement it fails.
Treating Youth and Rural and remote families as interchangeable with any Category B group.

sampleAnswers.answer: Priya’s choice partly meets the requirements, but it does not satisfy the course structure. The course requires two mandatory Category A groups, Youth and Rural and remote families. Priya has included Youth, which is correct, but she has omitted Rural and remote families, so the Category A requirement is not met. The course also requires two groups selected from Category B groups. Priya has chosen three Category B groups, Aged, Sole parents and Homeless people, so her selection exceeds the number allowed from that category. Her total of four groups is correct, which shows she understands the overall size of the study. To meet the requirements, Priya should replace one Category B group with Rural and remote families. This would give her two Category A groups and two Category B groups, as the course requires. Her choice therefore meets the total number of groups but fails the balance between the two categories.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: tests the choice against both category rules, identifies the missing Category A group and the surplus Category B group, and gives a sound judgement with a specific fix.

sampleAnswers.answer: Priya has included Youth, which is a mandatory Category A group. However, she has not included Rural and remote families, so she has not met the Category A requirement. She has chosen three Category B groups, which is one more than the course allows, so her selection does not fully meet the requirements.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains which requirements are met and not met, with some judgement. Adding a suggested change and a judgement on the overall extent would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Priya has chosen four groups, which is the correct total.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the number of groups with limited reference to the category requirements. Naming which requirement is not met would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Category A groups (Mandatory groups) (Youth; Rural and remote families)

prompts.question: Describe TWO ways in which living in a rural or remote area can shape the daily life of a family.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The Okafor family runs a sheep property about two hours’ drive from the nearest regional town, where the children attend school and the parents shop and see a doctor.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two ways that remoteness shapes a rural family’s daily life, with a clear link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies one way that remoteness affects a rural family, with limited description
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about rural and remote families
markerNotes: Give two separate ways, each with a short explanation of how it changes family routines or time.
Link each point to the Okafor family’s circumstances, such as travel to school or shops, rather than to rural life in general.
A list of rural features with no link to family life earns only the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the distance to services without saying how it changes the family’s daily life.
Giving one way and repeating it in different words, so that only one point is developed.
Writing about rural life in general instead of the family in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rural and remote families often travel long distances to reach schools, shops and health care, which limits their access to services and uses time and money each day. Family members may also share farm work, such as feeding stock or maintaining equipment, so the daily life of the family is shaped by the property rather than a town timetable, which affects the family’s wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes two ways that remoteness shapes daily life, each linked to the Okafor family. The points are developed rather than listed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Families in remote areas may have to drive a long way to reach a doctor or school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies one way that remoteness affects the family, with limited description. Explaining what the travel uses up, such as time or money, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Remote families may find it harder to get to services.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about rural and remote families. Describing one effect on the family’s daily routine would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the remote location of a family can affect the wellbeing of the young people within it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The Tran family lives on a property two hours from the nearest secondary school and a general practice. Their 15-year-old daughter, Linh, wants to play for a regional netball team that trains in a town an hour away.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how remoteness affects the physical and social wellbeing of a young person in the family, with sustained links to the scenario
5 marks: Analyses how remoteness affects the wellbeing of a young person, with clear links to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how the remote location affects a young person’s access to services or activities, with some link to wellbeing
3 marks: Describes an effect of remoteness on the family, with a limited link to wellbeing
2 marks: Identifies a feature of rural and remote living, with limited reference to the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about rural and remote families
markerNotes: Choose the young person and follow the effect through at least two dimensions of wellbeing, such as physical and social.
Show the mechanism: how distance or travel changes access to care or activities, and what that does to the young person.
Analysing one effect in depth earns more than listing several effects without links.
commonStudentErrors: Describing Linh’s netball or school in detail without explaining the effect on her wellbeing.
Stating that remote living is hard without naming the service or activity affected.
Writing about older family members when the question asks about young people.

sampleAnswers.answer: Linh’s wellbeing is affected by the family’s remote location in several connected ways, as a member of the Youth group within a Rural and remote families setting. Physical wellbeing may suffer when distance delays medical care, because the nearest general practice is far away and a minor injury or illness may not be treated quickly. Social wellbeing can be affected too: Linh’s place in netball, a major source of friendship and belonging, depends on her family finding time and fuel for a long round trip. The hours spent travelling may reduce the time Linh has for study and rest, which can affect her mental health and her sense of achievement. The parents may also carry the cost of transport, which adds financial pressure and can increase tension at home. Together these pressures can limit the opportunities Linh has to build the skills and relationships that support her wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: analyses the effect of remoteness on both physical and social wellbeing, using the scenario throughout. Each link runs from distance to access, and from access to Linh’s wellbeing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Linh’s netball is hard to attend because the town is an hour away, so she may miss sport and friends. The family also pays for fuel, which adds financial pressure. Distance from the doctor can delay treatment, which affects her physical wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains how the location affects access to an activity and to health care, with some link to wellbeing. Developing the social effect in more depth would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Living far away means Linh has fewer activities close to home, which can affect her wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a feature of remote living with limited reference to the scenario. Naming netball and the travel time would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Category B groups (Aged; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; People with disabilities; Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex, Asexual plus (LGBTQIA+) communities; Sole parents; Homeless people)

prompts.question: Outline how Category B groups differ from Category A groups in the requirements of this course.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is reading the course outline and wants to understand how many groups she must study from each category before she plans her research.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines that Category A groups are mandatory and that students select two groups from the Category B list
3 marks: Outlines the difference between the categories, naming the mandatory Category A groups
2 marks: Identifies that Category A groups are mandatory, with limited reference to Category B
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Category B groups
markerNotes: Set out the difference as a contrast: Category A is mandatory, and Category B is a selection from a list.
Name the Category B groups as examples of the selection, such as Aged or Homeless people, to show the list is known.
State the resulting pattern of two groups from each category so the requirement is complete.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that Category B groups are mandatory, which reverses the requirement.
Describing the groups in each category without explaining how the requirements differ.
Saying students choose any number of Category B groups rather than two.

sampleAnswers.answer: Category A groups are mandatory, so every student must study both Youth and Rural and remote families. Category B groups are a selection: students choose two groups from a list that includes Aged, Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, People with disabilities, LGBTQIA+ communities, Sole parents and Homeless people. The difference is that Category A is fixed, while Category B is a choice. Together, the requirement is two groups from each category, making four groups in total.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: outlines the contrast between a fixed mandatory category and a selected category, and states the resulting pattern of groups. The answer stays focused on the requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Category A groups are mandatory, so students must study Youth and Rural and remote families. Category B groups are chosen by the student from a list, rather than being fixed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: outlines the difference and names the mandatory Category A groups. Stating how many Category B groups a student selects would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Category B is a list of groups that students can choose from.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about Category B groups, but the contrast with Category A is not drawn. Stating that Category A groups are mandatory would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify the choice of TWO Category B groups that Mei should select for her study.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Mei lives in a regional town with a large retirement village and a growing number of families who speak languages other than English at home. She wants to choose two Category B groups that are most relevant to the community around her.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the choice of two Category B groups with sustained reasons linked to the community in the scenario and the specific needs of each group
5 marks: Justifies the choice of two Category B groups with clear reasons linked to the community in the scenario
4 marks: Explains a reason for each choice, with some link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes one of the chosen groups with a limited link to the community
2 marks: Identifies two Category B groups with limited reasons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Category B groups
markerNotes: Make a clear choice of two groups, then give a reason for each that draws on the scenario.
Show why the choice is relevant to this community, such as local services or the diversity within the groups.
A justification states why the choice is appropriate; a description of the groups alone does not justify it.
commonStudentErrors: Choosing two groups without giving any reason for the choice.
Describing the two groups in general instead of linking them to the community in the scenario.
Choosing a Category A group, which is not a choice from Category B.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mei should choose two Category B groups: Aged people and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities. The regional town has a large retirement village, so the specific needs of older residents, such as health care, housing and social connection, are visible in everyday community life. Mei could examine how well local services meet these needs and what the older residents themselves say. The growing number of families who speak other languages at home makes Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities equally relevant. Mei could examine how language and cultural background affect access to services, such as translated information or interpreters, and how the community responds. The two groups also differ in their diversity: older residents range from active retirees to people needing high levels of care, while families from many backgrounds have different needs and experiences. Studying two groups with such different characteristics allows Mei to compare how community structures respond to different needs, which makes her study well suited to this community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: justifies the choice of two groups with sustained reasons tied to the regional community, the specific needs of each group and the diversity within them. The answer makes a clear judgement rather than only describing the groups.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mei should choose Aged people, because the retirement village means many local residents are older. She could also choose Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities, because families speaking other languages live in the town. Both groups are relevant to the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: gives a reason for each choice with some link to the scenario. Explaining how each group’s specific needs affect services in the town would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mei could choose Aged people and Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies two Category B groups with limited reasons. Giving one reason for each choice from the scenario would lift it to the 3-mark row.

subTopics.name: Exploring the 4 (four) specific groups within the community

dotPoints.description: Prevalence of each group within the community; individual diversity within each group; terminology used by the community to describe the group

prompts.question: Describe how individuals can vary within the Homeless people group.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is researching homelessness in a regional city for an assignment. She wants to show that Homeless people are not one uniform group.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a range of ways in which individuals within the Homeless people group vary, with examples that show the diversity of circumstances
3 marks: Describes two ways in which individuals within the group vary, with limited examples
2 marks: Identifies a way in which individuals in the group differ, with limited description
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Homeless people
markerNotes: Give a range of circumstances, such as rough sleeping, staying with others or living in boarding houses, rather than one example.
Show that individuals differ in more than housing, for example in age, background or the reasons they lost their home.
Naming the categories without describing how individuals in each one differ earns only the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Describing homelessness as a single situation of sleeping on the street.
Listing types of housing without linking them to differences between individuals.
Describing the causes of homelessness rather than how individuals vary within the group.

sampleAnswers.answer: Homeless people do not share one set of circumstances, and this individual diversity matters for how the group is understood. Some people experience rough sleeping, living in cars, tents or public spaces. Others use crisis accommodation for short periods, or live in boarding houses where they have limited privacy. Many people experience couch surfing, staying with friends or relatives for short periods while their housing remains unstable. Individuals also vary in age, gender and cultural background, and in the reasons they lost their home, such as family breakdown, financial hardship or violence at home. These differences show why a single description of the group would be misleading.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes a range of circumstances with examples and links them to differences between individuals. The answer goes beyond housing type to include age, background and causes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some Homeless people sleep rough in cars or parks, while others stay with friends for a short time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies ways in which individuals differ, with limited description. Explaining how the differences affect the person’s needs would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Homeless people have different experiences of housing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information, but no specific difference is described. Giving one example of a different living situation would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the prevalence of Aged people in a community can inform the planning of services.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional council report shows that residents aged 75 and over make up a larger share of its population than the state average, and that this share is rising. Some of these residents are healthy and active, while others need high levels of care.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the prevalence of the group and its individual diversity together shape service planning, with sustained links to the scenario
5 marks: Analyses how the prevalence of the group can inform service planning, with clear links to the scenario
4 marks: Explains how the proportion of the group in the community affects service planning, with some reference to diversity
3 marks: Describes how a council might use data on the group, with a limited link to planning
2 marks: Identifies the prevalence of the group in the community, with limited reference to planning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Aged people
markerNotes: Explain the link from prevalence to planning: a larger share of the group means more demand for particular services.
Use the diversity within the group, such as the different care needs in the scenario, to show planning must not assume one need.
Stating that the group is large is only the first step; the analysis is in what the council must plan for.
commonStudentErrors: Stating the prevalence of the group without explaining how it affects planning.
Assuming all Aged people have the same needs and services.
Describing services for older people in general instead of how the data informs planning.

sampleAnswers.answer: The prevalence of Aged people shows the council how many residents are likely to need services in the future. In this scenario, the share of residents aged 75 and over is larger than the state average and is still rising, so demand for health care, aged care places and home support is likely to grow. Council planners can use this information to decide where to locate services, how many places to fund and when to expand them. However, prevalence alone can mislead if individual diversity is ignored. Some residents are healthy and active and may want social programs, transport and recreation, while others need high levels of care. Planning that treats all Aged people as needing the same support may leave the most dependent residents without help, or direct resources to people who are self-sufficient. A sound plan uses prevalence to estimate the overall demand and individual diversity to decide the mix of services, so the community responds to the real needs of its older residents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: analyses how prevalence informs the scale of demand, then uses individual diversity to refine the planning decision. The links to the scenario are sustained throughout.

sampleAnswers.answer: A larger share of Aged people in the community means the council must plan for more health care and home support. However, not all older residents need the same services, so planning should consider their different levels of care.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains how the proportion of the group affects planning, with some reference to diversity. Developing how the council would use the data in more detail would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The report shows that the share of residents aged 75 and over is higher than the state average.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the prevalence of the group with limited reference to planning. Explaining what the council would need to provide would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Utilise reliable sources of data to examine the nature of each group by considering the following questions: what is the prevalence of the group within Australia?; what determines whether an individual is part of the group?; how might individuals vary within the group?

prompts.question: Describe what determines whether an individual is part of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples group.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing a report on the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples group and wants to explain who belongs to it, without relying on stereotypes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes all three factors that determine group membership, descent, self-identification and community acceptance, with clear explanation of each
3 marks: Describes two factors that determine group membership, with some explanation
2 marks: Identifies one factor that determines group membership, with limited description
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples group
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
markerNotes: Name all three factors and explain each one, rather than listing them.
Show that membership is not decided by appearance or a single feature, which is the stereotype the scenario warns against.
Use the terms as the official definition uses them, since the question asks what determines membership.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that membership depends only on descent, without self-identification or community acceptance.
Describing physical features or appearance as determining membership.
Using stereotypes or generalisations about the group in place of the factors.

sampleAnswers.answer: An individual is part of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples group when three factors apply. First, the person is of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander descent. Second, the person identifies as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander, which is a personal choice about their own identity. Third, the person is accepted as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander by the community in which they live. Group membership is therefore decided by ancestry, self-identification and community acceptance together, not by appearance or any single feature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes all three factors and explains each one. The answer avoids appearance-based assumptions, which the scenario asks the student to avoid.

sampleAnswers.answer: Membership depends on being of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander descent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies one factor that determines membership, with limited description. Adding self-identification and community acceptance would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Membership of the group is based on a person’s identity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about membership, but the factors are not named. Naming descent or community acceptance would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify why a student should rely on reliable sources of data, rather than personal opinion, when examining how individuals vary within the Sole parents group.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has found two sources on Sole parents. One is a social media post describing all sole parents as struggling financially. The other is a national statistical release describing the household types and incomes of families across Australia.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the use of reliable sources of data with sustained reasons, showing how data reveals variation within the group that opinion cannot
5 marks: Justifies the use of reliable sources of data with clear reasons linked to variation within the group
4 marks: Explains a reason for using reliable data, with some link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a difference between the two sources, with limited justification
2 marks: Identifies one source and a feature of sole parents, with limited reasons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about sole parents
markerNotes: Justify with reasons that the data shows variation, such as different incomes or household types, rather than a single view.
Contrast the two sources in the scenario and explain why one can support conclusions and the other cannot.
Stating that data is better is not enough; explain what the data reveals about individual diversity.
commonStudentErrors: Saying data is more accurate without explaining what it shows about the group.
Describing the sole parents group in general without linking to variation between individuals.
Treating the social media post as equally reliable because it describes real people.

sampleAnswers.answer: A student should rely on reliable sources of data because they reveal the variation within the Sole parents group, which personal opinion cannot. The social media post describes all sole parents as struggling financially, which is a generalisation that ignores individual diversity. Sole parents may be separated, widowed or never partnered, and they may be men or women working full-time, part-time or not at all. A national statistical release can show the range of household types and incomes, so the student can see how many sole parents are in different situations and how common each situation is. This provides a prevalence figure that is tested against a defined method, rather than a single account. Relying on the data also protects the student from stereotypes, because the conclusions follow from evidence about the whole group. For these reasons, the statistical release is the stronger source for examining how individuals vary.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: justifies the use of reliable data with sustained reasons, showing that it reveals the variation the opinion post hides. The contrast between the two sources is clear and developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: A student should use reliable data because it shows how many sole parents are in different situations. The social media post only describes one view of sole parents, so it cannot show variation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains a reason for using reliable data, with some link to the scenario. Explaining the range of variation the data reveals, such as household types or incomes, would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A national statistical release is a source of data about sole parents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a source with limited reasons. Explaining why the data is more reliable than the post would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Recognise that the community uses positive and negative terminology to describe each group. Discuss the impact this might have on individuals within the group

prompts.question: Describe one positive and one negative term the community uses to describe Aged people.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is comparing how local media and community groups describe older residents for a class presentation on terminology.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes one positive and one negative term, explaining how each shapes community perceptions of Aged people
3 marks: Describes one positive and one negative term, with limited explanation of their effect
2 marks: Identifies a term used for Aged people, with limited description of its tone
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about terms used for Aged people
markerNotes: Name one term for each side and say what it suggests about older people, rather than only quoting the words.
Explain how the community perception shapes the way Aged people are treated.
Use terms the community actually uses, and describe their tone, rather than inventing offensive language.
commonStudentErrors: Giving two positive terms, or two negative ones, instead of one of each.
Naming a term without saying whether it is positive or negative.
Describing the age of older people rather than the terminology used.

sampleAnswers.answer: A positive term is ‘older Australians’, which presents people as a valued part of the community and avoids focusing only on age-related decline. A negative term is describing older people as ‘a burden on the health system’, which presents Aged people as a cost rather than as contributors. Such terminology can suggest that older people are less useful than younger people, and it can shape community attitudes towards them. Positive terminology supports respect and inclusion, while negative terminology can reduce the opportunities Aged people are offered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes one positive and one negative term and explains how each shapes community perceptions. The answer links the terms to the treatment of Aged people.

sampleAnswers.answer: Calling older people ‘a burden’ is a negative term that suggests they are a cost.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a negative term with limited description. Adding a positive term and explaining its effect would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The community uses words such as ‘senior’ to describe older people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about the terminology, but the tone is not described. Stating whether the term is positive or negative would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss the impact that negative terminology could have on the wellbeing of individuals within the Youth group.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A local newspaper repeatedly describes groups of teenagers at the skate park as ‘trouble’. A 16-year-old in the area says that classmates now call him a ‘troublemaker’ whenever he walks past the park.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the impact of negative terminology on the wellbeing of young people, weighing its effects on identity, relationships and behaviour, with sustained links to the scenario
5 marks: Discusses the impact of negative terminology on wellbeing, with clear links to the scenario
4 marks: Explains an effect of negative terminology on young people, with some link to wellbeing
3 marks: Describes a way the label could affect a young person, with limited link to wellbeing
2 marks: Identifies negative terminology used about young people, with limited reference to impact
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the Youth group
markerNotes: Follow the impact through at least two areas, such as sense of identity and relationships, and show how the label affects each.
Include a balanced point, such as a young person who rejects the label but is still affected by repeated exposure to it.
Connect the impact to the scenario, the newspaper and classmates, rather than writing about young people in general.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the negative terms without discussing their impact on wellbeing.
Stating that negative terms always cause harm, without any reasoning or balance.
Writing about bullying in general instead of the effect of the terminology in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Negative terminology can affect the wellbeing of young people in the Youth group by shaping how they see themselves. In the scenario, the newspaper’s repeated use of ‘trouble’ may lead the 16-year-old to accept the label, which can damage his sense of identity and self-esteem. When classmates use ‘troublemaker’ as a routine name, it can change his relationships, as he may avoid the skate park and the peers who are there. This avoidance can reduce his opportunities for exercise, friendship and belonging, which are important to his wellbeing. The label can also influence behaviour: a young person who feels judged may act in ways that confirm the description. Some young people may reject the label and dismiss it, but repeated exposure can still affect how they are treated by adults and peers. On balance, negative terminology tends to reduce wellbeing because it limits how young people are seen and what they are expected to become.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: discusses the impact on identity, relationships and behaviour, weighs a counter-view, and links every point to the scenario. The judgement is sustained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Being called a troublemaker may affect how the 16-year-old sees himself, which can reduce his confidence. He may also avoid the skate park to avoid the label, so he has fewer chances to socialise with friends.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains an effect on identity and social life, with some link to wellbeing. Adding a balanced point or a second area of impact would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Newspapers and classmates use negative words such as ‘trouble’ about young people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies negative terminology with limited reference to its impact. Explaining how the label affects the young person would lift it to the 3-mark row.

subTopics.name: Issues of concern for the 4 (four) specific groups within the community

dotPoints.description: Satisfaction of needs (specific needs of each group (adequate standard of living (food, clothing, shelter); health; education; employment; safety and security; sense of identity))

prompts.question: Outline TWO specific needs of People with disabilities that relate to health and to safety and security.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Daniel uses a wheelchair following a spinal injury and lives in a rented flat on the third floor of a building without a lift.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines two specific needs of People with disabilities, each linked to health or to safety and security, with relevant detail
3 marks: Outlines two specific needs of People with disabilities, with limited detail
2 marks: Identifies one specific need of People with disabilities, with a brief outline
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the needs of People with disabilities
markerNotes: Name one need linked to health and one linked to safety and security, and outline what meeting each need involves.
Use the scenario, such as the building without a lift, to make the need specific rather than general.
Describing the disability itself is not a need; the answer should show what the person requires.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a need without explaining what it involves.
Describing the injury or disability rather than the need that follows from it.
Giving two needs that both relate to health, when the question asks for one of each.

sampleAnswers.answer: One of the specific needs of People with disabilities is health care, including regular medical review and access to physiotherapy and equipment that supports daily mobility, such as Daniel’s wheelchair. Meeting this need supports his physical wellbeing and reduces the risk of complications. A second need is safety and security in the home. Because Daniel’s flat is on the third floor of a building without a lift, he needs accessible housing or a safe means of leaving the building in an emergency. Without this, his safety and security are at risk.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: outlines two specific needs, one linked to health and one to safety and security, each with relevant detail from the scenario. The answer is brief and well matched to 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Daniel needs health care to manage his injury and his mobility.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies one specific need with a brief outline. Adding the safety and security need, linked to the building, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: People with disabilities have health needs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information, but no specific need is outlined. Naming one need and what it involves would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how meeting the education and employment needs of a sole parent can influence the wellbeing of the family.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Jade is a sole parent of two primary school children. She left school early and works part-time in retail while studying through a community-based training course.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how meeting education and employment needs affects the wellbeing of the sole parent and family, with sustained links to the scenario and the adequate standard of living
5 marks: Analyses how meeting these needs affects wellbeing, with clear links to the scenario
4 marks: Explains one effect of meeting an education or employment need on the family, with some link to wellbeing
3 marks: Describes an education or employment need of the sole parent, with a limited link to wellbeing
2 marks: Identifies an education or employment need, with limited reference to the family
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about sole parents
markerNotes: Follow the chain from a need being met (training or work) to a change in income, time or confidence, then to the family’s wellbeing.
Show that the effect is two-sided: work or study can also reduce time for children, so analyse both.
Use the scenario details, such as the two children and the training course, rather than sole parents in general.
commonStudentErrors: Describing education and employment without explaining how they affect wellbeing.
Stating that work is always good for wellbeing, without analysing the time or stress it adds.
Writing about the children’s education rather than the sole parent’s needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Meeting the specific needs of a sole parent, such as Jade’s education and employment needs, can improve the wellbeing of her family in several connected ways. Her training course may lead to qualifications that allow her to move from part-time retail into more secure work with higher pay. Higher and more stable income would help meet the adequate standard of living for the household, reducing financial stress on the two children and on Jade. Her own confidence and sense of achievement may also grow as she gains skills, which supports her emotional wellbeing. However, study and work take time, and the family may have less time together or less supervision after school. The analysis therefore depends on how Jade manages her time, including support from school programs or family members. If the needs are met with adequate childcare and flexible hours, the family is more likely to gain overall wellbeing. Without that support, the same education and employment could increase stress and reduce the time available for parenting.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: analyses how meeting education and employment needs affects income, confidence and family time, and weighs both sides. The links to the scenario are sustained.

sampleAnswers.answer: If Jade completes her training, she may be able to work more hours in better-paid work. This can help the household meet its basic costs, which lowers financial stress for the family.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains one effect of meeting an employment need on the family, with some link to wellbeing. Adding the effect on her confidence or the family’s time would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Jade is studying and working part-time while she raises her children.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies education and employment needs with limited reference to the family. Explaining what the training would change for the household would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Identify and prioritise the specific needs of each group

prompts.question: Extract THREE specific needs of Walter, an Aged person, from the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Walter is 81 and lives alone in a two-storey house. He has a heart condition, relies on his neighbour to shop for food, and worries about paying rent from his pension. He also feels isolated since his wife died and worries about falling on the stairs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Extracts three specific needs of Walter, each accurately drawn from the scenario
2 marks: Extracts two specific needs of Walter from the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information from the scenario about Walter
markerNotes: Name each need in the category it belongs to, such as health or safety and security, and tie it to a detail in the scenario.
Extract needs rather than problems: the answer should say what Walter requires, not only what he worries about.
Three distinct needs from three different categories earn more than three details from one category.
commonStudentErrors: Copying sentences from the scenario without naming the need they show.
Naming needs that are not in the scenario, such as transport, which is not raised.
Naming the same need twice, such as health and heart condition.

sampleAnswers.answer: As an aged person, Walter has three specific needs. Health: regular medical care to manage his heart condition. Safety and security: a safe home, since he risks falling on the stairs of his two-storey house. Adequate standard of living: enough food, supported by his neighbour’s shopping, and affordable housing, given his concern about paying rent from his pension.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: extracts three distinct needs from three categories, each tied to a detail in the scenario. The answer identifies needs rather than retelling the story.

sampleAnswers.answer: Health: medical care for his heart condition. Safety and security: a safe home for someone at risk of falling.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: extracts two specific needs accurately. Adding a third need from the scenario, such as food or housing, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Walter lives alone in a two-storey house.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information from the scenario, but no need is extracted. Naming a need that the detail shows would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify which TWO specific needs should be prioritised for Walter, using evidence from the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Walter is 81 and lives alone in a two-storey house. He has a heart condition, relies on his neighbour to shop for food, and worries about paying rent from his pension. He also feels isolated since his wife died and worries about falling on the stairs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the prioritisation of two specific needs with sustained reasons, weighing the urgency and consequences of each need using evidence from the scenario
5 marks: Justifies the prioritisation of two specific needs with clear reasons drawn from the scenario
4 marks: Explains why one priority need matters for Walter, with some use of evidence
3 marks: Describes a need that Walter has, with limited reasons for its priority
2 marks: Identifies a specific need of Walter, with limited reference to priority
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Walter’s needs
markerNotes: Choose two needs and rank them by urgency or consequence, then give evidence from the scenario for each choice.
Show how the two priorities support each other, such as safety reducing the risk of hospital admission.
A priority justified only by how serious the need sounds, with no evidence, earns the middle rows.
commonStudentErrors: Choosing two needs without giving a reason why they come first.
Prioritising the need that is easiest to meet rather than the one with the greatest risk.
Using evidence that is not in the scenario, such as Walter’s family visiting him.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two most important specific needs for Walter to prioritise are health and safety and security. His heart condition is an immediate risk to his wellbeing, because an untreated episode could lead to a serious medical emergency. Regular care is therefore urgent, and it should come before needs that can wait. His risk of falling on the stairs of a two-storey house is linked to the same concern. A fall could cause injury, lead to hospital admission and make it harder for him to look after his health. Addressing the stairs and the risk of falling would protect both his physical health and his independence in his own home. Adequate standard of living matters, but his neighbour already helps with shopping, so the need for food is partly met for now. Rent worries are real, yet they do not carry the same immediate risk to his life. Prioritising health and safety therefore addresses the needs with the most serious and immediate consequences for Walter.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: justifies two priorities by weighing urgency and consequences, with evidence from the scenario at each step. The reasons for setting aside the other needs are clear.

sampleAnswers.answer: Walter should prioritise health, because his heart condition is a serious risk that needs regular medical care. Without this, his condition could worsen quickly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains why one priority matters, with some use of evidence. Adding the second priority and a reason for its place would lift it to the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Walter’s health and safety are important needs for him.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies specific needs with limited reference to priority. Giving a reason why one need is more urgent than the others would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Justify the 2 (two) most significant needs for each group and discuss the implications if these are not met

prompts.question: Explain the implications for youth when their significant needs are not met. Use examples to support your answer.
markerNotes: Choose two significant needs for young people and explain the consequence of each going unmet, then tie each consequence to wellbeing.
Give at least two concrete examples, such as a young person who is excluded from school or who feels no sense of belonging, and show how each example produces the implication.
commonStudentErrors: Listing all six needs without choosing two or explaining why they are significant for youth.
Naming an implication, such as being unhappy, without explaining the chain of effects that leads to it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of the implications for youth when their significant needs are not met; Includes detailed examples
6-7 marks: Provides a sound explanation of the implications for youth when their significant needs are not met; Includes relevant examples
4-5 marks: Provides some explanation of the implications for youth when their significant needs are not met; Includes examples
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of significant need(s) of youth
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Sense of identity allows youth to be more empowered to make stronger life decisions and healthy choices. Without a clear sense of identity and belonging, youth may experience social isolation. Feeling disconnected from peers and community can lead to loneliness, depression, and an increased vulnerability to negative influences such as risky behaviours or unhealthy relationships. Education is vital for the development of knowledge and skills and opens opportunities for employment. If educational needs are not met, it can hinder academic performance and the development of essential skills. A lack of engagement in the learning process may result in decreased motivation, and a higher likelihood of dropping out of school. Unmet educational needs can limit career options and economic prospects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row for the explanation and the examples, using two needs with clear consequences. The link to wellbeing is implied and would be stronger if stated for each consequence.

sampleAnswers.answer: When young people's needs are not met, they may find it hard to make good choices. For example, a young person who does not feel safe at home or in their neighbourhood may become anxious, and this can affect their school attendance. Missing school can then make it harder to find work later, which limits their independence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the some-explanation row: it explains one implication with an example and traces a chain to a second, but the wellbeing effect is brief and only one need is developed. Developing a second need with a specific example would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people who do not get their needs met may feel unhappy and may not do well at school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the some-understanding row: it recognises that unmet needs cause problems, but names no specific need and gives no example.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Access to services (types of services, eg financial support, transport, accommodation and housing, health care, counselling, education, employment, legal aid; factors affecting access to services (characteristics of individuals within the group, eg age, gender, level of education, culture, type of disability, first language spoken, socioeconomic status; resources, eg time, money, energy, knowledge; aspects of the service, eg opening hours, confidentiality, location, staffing))

prompts.question: Explain how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to the services.
markerNotes: Name one aspect of the service, such as opening hours, location, staffing or confidentiality, and explain how it limits access for rural and remote families.
Connect each aspect to the family situation, such as farm work or long travel, so the explanation shows the effect rather than the feature.
Explaining two aspects in depth separates a sound answer from one that only lists aspects.
commonStudentErrors: Describing services in remote areas without naming an aspect of the service that affects access.
Explaining the difficulties of rural life in general rather than how aspects of services affect access.
Naming location or staffing as a problem without saying why it matters for the family.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Provides a comprehensive explanation of how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to services
6 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to services
4-5 marks: Provides sound explanation of how aspects of services can affect rural and remote families’ access to services
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of aspects of services and/or how they affect rural and remote families’ access to services
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Staffing – rural and remote areas are more likely to experience a skills shortage. For acute health issues such as crush farming injuries, there may not be trained or experienced staff. Online financial support services can be accessed when convenient, however if metropolitan based, they may lack knowledge of remote issues, such as drought specific rebates.
Confidentiality – keeping personal matters private can be challenging due to the size of communities. In smaller communities, family members may be less likely to disclose sensitive but necessary health information to health services, for fear of judgement or shame, leading to worsening health condition.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains how staffing and confidentiality affect access for rural and remote families, with a clear reason for each. Both aspects are developed fully, which is what the top row asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: Services may be open only during business hours, which clashes with work on the farm during busy seasons, so rural families may have to choose between a service and their work or miss out on care altogether. Travel to services can also be costly for the family.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: gives a sound explanation of one aspect, that services are 'open only during business hours', which clashes with farm work, while travel is named but not explained. Developing the travel point, such as the time and cost to the family, would lift it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Services in the country are often far away, so families have to drive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some understanding of a feature of services and its effect, but the explanation is brief and the aspect is not named. Explaining why distance limits access, such as the time and fuel cost, would move it up.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

prompts.question: Describe how ONE service can assist people with disabilities.
markerNotes: Name one service and say what it provides for a person with a disability, such as income, equipment or home modifications, rather than only naming the service.
Link the service to a specific need, such as an adequate standard of living or safety, so the description shows how the service assists.
The question asks for ONE service. Develop that one with examples; a second service adds length without adding marks.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a service, such as a support payment, without describing how it assists people with a disability.
Describing the disability itself, rather than what the service does for the person.
Listing several services with one line each, so that none is described in enough detail.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Provides a thorough description of how ONE service that can assist people with disabilities
3 marks: Provides a sound description of how ONE service that can assist people with disabilities
2 marks: Provides a basic description of service(s) that can assist people with disabilities
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: People with a disability can access financial support with a government disability support payment to assist with everyday necessities such as accommodation and food if they are unable to work. This financial support can also provide them with specialised equipment such as wheelchairs and home modifications, for example, shower rails.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes one service, a government disability support payment, and how it assists with accommodation, food and specialised equipment. The answer is brief and well matched to 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A government payment gives people with a disability money to cover basic living costs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: a basic description of one service that can assist people with disability. Explaining what the money lets the person do, such as keep a home or buy equipment, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some services help people with a disability.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information, but no service is described and it is not clear how it helps. Naming one service and what it provides would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Explore the factors that can affect each group’s access to services by considering the following questions: what types of services does each group require access to?; how do the characteristics of individuals within each group affect their access to services?; what resources are necessary to support each group’s access to the service?; how available are the services within the community?

prompts.question: How could the characteristics of individuals living in a rural and remote location affect a family’s access to services?
markerNotes: Choose two or three characteristics, such as socioeconomic status, age or disability, and show how each changes a family's ability to reach a service in a rural or remote setting.
Link each characteristic to a specific service, such as specialist health care or counselling, rather than describing rural life in general.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the distance to services without linking it to the characteristics of individuals.
Listing characteristics such as age and gender without explaining how each one affects access.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Demonstrates a thorough understanding of how the characteristics of individuals living in a rural and remote location affect a family’s access to services
6 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of how the characteristics of individuals living in a rural and remote location affect a family’s access to services
4-5 marks: Demonstrates an understanding of how the characteristics of individuals living in a rural and remote location affect a family’s access to services
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of characteristic(s) of individuals in rural and remote families and/or their access to service(s)
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Individuals from rural and remote families may have a lower socioeconomic status during times of drought, flood, or unproductive farming periods. During this time of hardship, finances may be quite low affecting individual’s ability to access high fee health services such as dental, specialist doctor appointments or private health insurance. During such times an individual may neglect to use any of these services due to their expensive nature, possibly leading to further chronic health conditions. A person with a physical disability in a rural or remote area may have a reduced choice of specialised health services and may have to travel long distances to access physiotherapy or rehabilitation. This extended travel time will be expensive and tiresome for the person as it may require specialist transport services or a support person.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the sound-understanding row: it links socioeconomic status and disability to specific services, such as specialist health care and physiotherapy. Explaining how travel costs compound low income would take it to the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Families in rural and remote areas may have lower incomes, especially during drought, so they may not afford specialist health services. Older people may also have less access to services because they cannot travel long distances. A family on a low income may have to choose between paying for a specialist and other essentials, so the visit is put off or skipped altogether.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 mark row: demonstrates an understanding of how low income and age affect access, and that a family 'may have to choose between paying for a specialist' and other essentials. Explaining how travel costs compound low income, and naming a specific service such as physiotherapy, would take it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rural families sometimes find it hard to get services because they live far away.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the some-understanding row: it notes some difficulty for rural families but names no characteristic of individuals. Linking distance to a characteristic, such as the cost of travel for a family on a low income, would lift it.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

prompts.question: Explain the characteristics that may affect a student’s access to counselling services.
markerNotes: Explain each characteristic as a barrier or support to access, such as age affecting whether a student needs parental consent, rather than listing it.

Use the characteristics named in the syllabus (age, socioeconomic status, level of education, culture, first language) and say how each one changes what the student can use, such as time, money or knowledge.
A thorough answer shows the mechanism, for example a student who works long hours has less time to attend face-to-face sessions.
commonStudentErrors: Listing characteristics without explaining how each one affects access.
Describing the benefits of counselling instead of the characteristics that affect access to it.
Writing about the student’s mental health problem as the characteristic, rather than the factors that change how easily they can get help.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of a student’s characteristics that may affect their access to counselling services; Provides relevant examples
4 marks: Provides a sound explanation of a student’s characteristics that may affect their access to counselling services; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Provides some information about a student’s characteristics that may affect their access to counselling services
1 mark: Provides relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Characteristics such as age, socioeconomic status and level of education may affect a student’s access to counselling. Due to their age, an older student may have the ability to drive to face-to-face counselling and parental consent may not be required making it easier to access the service.
Counselling can be an expensive service. The student may manage employment along with study commitments and this could limit income potential, thus negatively affecting their ability to access this service.
Counselling services can be promoted in an educational institution to support student wellbeing. This would increase level of knowledge about counselling services that exist, such as headspace, which are easy to access via phone, face to face or online.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains several characteristics (age, socioeconomic status and education) and how each affects access to counselling, with examples that show the mechanism.

sampleAnswers.answer: Age and income can affect whether a student can get counselling. A student with a part-time job may not have time to attend an appointment during the day, because their working hours clash with the times the service is open. Income matters too, since a student who cannot afford the travel or a private session may not go at all.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: names age and income, with a student 'with a part-time job' as the example, but the explanation of how each characteristic changes access is brief. Explaining why age changes access, and adding a second characteristic, would lift it to the 4-5 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Students may not know that counselling services exist.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: relevant information about counselling, but no characteristic of the student is named. Naming one characteristic and how it changes access would lift it to the 2-3 row.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Addressing the groups’ issues of concern (government policy and legislation; organisations within the community that support the group; equity issues)

prompts.question: Explain how a community organisation supports the rights of ONE of the following Category B groups.
markerNotes: Name one specific community organisation and say which right of the group it supports, such as access to basic health and hygiene.
Explain the mechanism: how the organisation's service or action gives members of the group that right in practice.
Stay with the one group chosen; a second group adds length without earning marks.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the group needs or disadvantages without naming an organisation or explaining how it helps.
Naming a government agency or an Act when the question asks about a community organisation.
Listing several organisations without explaining how any one of them supports the group's rights.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of how a community organisation supports the rights of the group
5 marks: Provides a sound explanation of how a community organisation supports the rights of the group
4 marks: Provides an explanation of how a community organisation supports the rights of the group
3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of a way a community organisation has attempted to support the rights of the group
2 marks: Provides some understanding of a community organisation and/or rights of the group
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Group: Homeless people
Orange Sky is a community organisation that supports the rights of homeless people to access basic health and hygiene. Some homeless people are rough sleepers, using makeshift dwellings like tents, derelict buildings or cars and have limited access to shower and laundry facilities.
