This organisation has easily distinguishable orange vans containing shower and laundry facilities, that frequent known areas of rough sleepers. This means the members of this group can wash and feel clean, reducing risk of infection, and can have their clothes cleaned and dried.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains how a named organisation gives homeless people access to a basic right, with the reason its vans reach rough sleepers. The explanation stays on the question and links the service to the group wellbeing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Orange Sky is a community organisation that gives homeless people access to showers and laundry, so they can keep clean. Its vans visit the places where rough sleepers stay, which makes the service easy to reach.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: shows some understanding of one way Orange Sky supports homeless people, by giving access to showers and laundry, and says its vans 'visit the places where rough sleepers stay', but does not explain how this supports a right. Explaining how this affects health would move it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations help homeless people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information, but no organisation is named and no right is explained. Naming one organisation and what it provides would lift it to the 3-mark row.

prompts.scenario: [Category B groups, listed in two columns on the paper: Aged; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples; People with disabilities; Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex, Asexual plus (LGBTQIA+) communities; Sole parents; Homeless people]
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Examine government policy and legislation to determine its role in ensuring equity for each group

prompts.question: Answer the question in relation to ONE of the following Category B groups. To what extent does legislation ensure equity for the diverse members within this group? Use specific examples of legislation to support your answer.
markerNotes: Judge the extent: say how far the legislation delivers equity and where it falls short, then take a position rather than describing the Act.
Diversity within the group is what the question tests; show that the legislation helps some members more than others, such as by type of disability.
Name the legislation accurately and link each Act to a specific effect on equity, with an example of how it works in practice.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what the legislation says without judging how far it ensures equity.
Treating the group as one uniform group and ignoring the diversity within it.
Listing several Acts without explaining what each one does for equity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides valid judgement on the extent to which legislation ensures equity for the diversity within one of the groups; Provides detailed examples
6-7 marks: Provides judgement on the extent to which legislation ensures equity for the diversity within one of the groups; Provides relevant examples
4-5 marks: Attempts to provide judgement on how legislation contributes to equity and/or diversity within one of the groups; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of legislation in relation to equity and/or diversity within one of the groups
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Group: People with disabilities
The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (DDA) makes it unlawful to discriminate against a person based on disability in many areas of life, including the workplace. The broad definition of a disability can impact the identification of and successful implementation of reasonable adjustments to support inclusion.
For those with a physical disability that can be seen visually, installing ramps can be understood and easily implemented without judgement, increasing equity of access. For those with a psychosocial disability or illness, the nature of the workplace adjustment such as flexible work arrangements may inadvertently lead colleagues to gossip, ask questions and speculate, which may lead to indirect discrimination. Therefore, the DDA may have some success in creating equity. However, there is still considerable inequity across the diversity of the group based on an individual’s disability category.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: makes a valid judgement that the Disability Discrimination Act creates some equity but leaves inequity across disability types, supported by detailed examples of ramps and psychosocial disability. The judgement is clear and is returned to in the final sentence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation such as the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 makes it unlawful to discriminate against people with disability at work and in other areas. For example, an employer may need to make reasonable adjustments. This helps some people with disability, but not all of them, so the law is only partly effective.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: attempts a judgement on how the legislation contributes to equity, with an example. The judgement is stated but not supported, and the diversity within the group is not explored. Explaining why the law helps a physical disability more than a psychosocial one would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation such as the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 protects people with disability from unfair treatment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some understanding of legislation and equity for the group, but no judgement and no example. Adding an example of how the Act works in practice would move it to the 4-5 row.

prompts.scenario: [Category B groups, listed in two columns on the paper: Aged; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples; People with disabilities; Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex, Asexual plus (LGBTQIA+) communities; Sole parents; Homeless people]
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Critically analyse the extent to which organisations within the community assist in satisfying the needs of each group

prompts.question: Describe how ONE community organisation can assist Rural and remote families to satisfy their need for education.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A community organisation in a regional town runs a free tutoring and online learning centre for students whose families live on properties more than an hour from the nearest high school.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes how ONE community organisation assists Rural and remote families to meet their education needs, with specific detail on the support it provides
3 marks: Describes how ONE community organisation assists Rural and remote families, with limited detail
2 marks: Identifies a community organisation that assists with education, with limited description
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about education for Rural and remote families
markerNotes: Name one organisation type and describe what it does for the families, such as tutoring or online access.
Link the support to the remoteness of the families, such as travel time or study around farm work.
The question asks for ONE organisation; developing one in depth earns more than listing several.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a school or government department rather than a community organisation.
Naming an organisation without describing how it assists education.
Describing education in rural areas in general without the organisation.

sampleAnswers.answer: This community organisation runs a tutoring and online learning centre that students from rural and remote families can attend when they cannot reach a school easily. Tutors help students keep up with set work and prepare for assessments, while online access lets students study at times that suit farm work and long travel. The organisation may also lend computers or provide internet access to families who lack them. This meets the specific needs of students whose education would otherwise be affected by isolation and distance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes one community organisation, what it provides and how that meets the education needs of rural and remote families. The answer is brief and specific.

sampleAnswers.answer: The organisation offers tutoring to students in a regional town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a community organisation that assists with education, with limited description. Explaining how the tutoring helps families who live far from school would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A community organisation can help students with schoolwork.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about education, but the families are not identified. Naming rural and remote families as the group would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Critically analyse the extent to which community organisations assist Homeless people in satisfying their specific needs.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A city council report states that three community organisations provide meals, short-term accommodation and health outreach to Homeless people. However, the services close by 4pm, are based only in the inner city, and rely on donations that vary from year to year.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Critically analyses the extent to which community organisations meet the specific needs of Homeless people, with sustained judgement supported by integrated evidence from the scenario
6 marks: Critically analyses the extent of assistance from community organisations, with a sound judgement supported by relevant evidence
5 marks: Analyses how community organisations assist Homeless people, with some judgement on the extent of that assistance
3-4 marks: Describes services provided by community organisations, with limited analysis of their extent
2 marks: Identifies a community organisation that assists Homeless people, with limited description
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Homeless people or community organisations
markerNotes: Judge the extent by weighing what the organisations provide against what the group still needs, such as timing, location and funding.
Use the limits in the scenario as evidence: a service that closes at 4pm does not meet every need for every person.
Describing services is the middle of the range; the top rows need an explicit judgement on how far the needs are satisfied.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the services in the scenario without judging how far they satisfy the needs.
Claiming the organisations fully meet all needs without evidence.
Discussing government policy rather than the community organisations asked about.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations make a substantial contribution to the specific needs of Homeless people, although their assistance is uneven. The meals and short-term accommodation address the adequate standard of living, because food and a safe place to sleep are immediate needs. Health outreach responds to the health needs of people who may not otherwise see a doctor, and this is an important form of access. However, the extent of assistance is limited by timing. Services that close by 4pm do not help people who need shelter overnight or who are working during the day, so some needs remain unmet. Location is a second limit: services based only in the inner city are difficult to reach for people who live in outer suburbs or who have no transport. Funding is a third limit, because donations that vary from year to year make it hard to plan long-term accommodation, which is the need most tied to safety and security. Organisations also differ in the people they reach, so the needs of individuals with complex conditions may receive less support than those of people who can attend. On balance, the organisations meet basic and immediate needs well, but they satisfy the specific needs of Homeless people only partly, because the services are not consistently available, accessible or sustained.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: gives a sustained judgement on the extent of assistance, supported by evidence about timing, location and funding. The answer weighs what is met against what remains unmet.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations provide meals, short-term accommodation and health outreach, which assist Homeless people with basic needs. The services close early and are based in the inner city, so they may not reach everyone who needs them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: analyses how the organisations assist, with some judgement on their limits. Developing the judgement, with evidence on funding and the groups who miss out, would lift it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A community organisation provides meals to Homeless people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a community organisation that assists the group, with limited description. Describing the other services and their limits would lift it to the 3-4 mark row.

dotPoints.description: Investigate a current inequity issue faced by each group and propose strategies to address the issue

prompts.question: Answer the question in relation to ONE Category B group you have studied. Explain strategies that could be implemented to enhance equity for your chosen group.
markerNotes: Choose one inequity the group faces, such as limited access to care, and explain one or more strategies that would address it, rather than listing strategies.
Explain how each strategy would enhance equity for the group, such as by improving access to a service or the income the group needs.
Say who would carry out each strategy, such as government, employers or community organisations, and how that would reach the group.
commonStudentErrors: Explaining strategies for equity in general, rather than for the chosen group.
Listing strategies, such as more funding, without explaining how each would enhance equity.
Naming an inequity without linking it to a strategy that would address it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of strategies that could be implemented to enhance equity for the chosen group
6 marks: Provides a sound explanation of strategies that could be implemented to enhance equity for the chosen group
4-5 marks: Provides an explanation of one or more strategies that could be implemented to enhance equity for the chosen group
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding about equity issues for the chosen group
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Group: Aged
Strategies that could help to improve health inequities could be increasing wages, upskilling and the promotion of younger people to enter the workforce in careers that are in aged care. This will not only be effective in helping to improve the health care needs of the aged but also will ultimately help to establish positive attitudes amongst the youth when working with the aged. The government could also increase funding further in areas of need such as the Aged Pension as well as improving support to community organisations which assist the aged. This will be beneficial in improving equitable access to specific resources and services, such as counselling services and improving their emotional wellbeing. Finally, workplaces could have programs which allow the aged to slowly move out of the workforce into part-time work. This would be essential in maintaining an income to support their needs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains several strategies for the aged, including workforce programs, government funding and support for community organisations, and links each to equitable access to services and to wellbeing. The answer is well matched to 7 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: One strategy is for the government to fund more in-home care, so older people can stay in their own homes and keep their independence. Government funding would mean older people on a low income can receive help with daily tasks such as cooking and bathing without having to move into residential care. This allows them to remain connected to their own neighbourhood and community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 mark row: explains one strategy, to 'fund more in-home care', and how it lets older people stay independent at home. Adding a second strategy, or linking the strategy to a specific equity issue such as rural access, would lift it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government could give older people more money.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 mark row: some understanding of equity issues for the aged, with a general strategy and no explanation. Explaining what the money would pay for and how that improves equity would lift it to the 4-5 mark row.

prompts.scenario: [Category B groups, listed in two columns on the paper: Aged; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; Rural and remote families; Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Transgender, Intersex communities; Sole parents; Homeless people]
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Positive influences on community attitudes (contributions the group makes within the community; advocacy (speaking up for the group’s needs and concerns) (raising awareness within the community; educating the community; promoting the rights of the group))

prompts.question: Answer the question in relation to ONE Category B group you have studied. Analyse the contribution the group makes within the wider community.
markerNotes: Analyse the contribution rather than describing the group: say what the group does, what the community gains, and how this links to the wider community.
Use a specific named organisation or activity as an example, such as a volunteer program, so the contribution is shown in practice.
Top answers link the contribution to community attitudes or wellbeing, which is the analysis the 8-mark row asks for.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the needs or problems of the group instead of its contribution to the community.
Writing a general statement that the group contributes, with no example or analysis.
Describing the group in negative or stereotyped terms rather than the contribution it makes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding about the contribution the group makes within the wider community; Provides an extensive analysis of the contribution the group makes within the wider community; Provides relevant examples
6-7 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding about the contribution the group makes within the wider community; Provides a thorough analysis of the contribution the group makes within the wider community; Provides examples
4-5 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding about the contribution the group makes within the wider community; Provides a link between the contribution and the wider community; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Provides basic information about the group and/or its contribution within the wider community
1 mark: Provides relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The aged population comprises individuals over the age of 65 some of which are retired.
Many aged people volunteer for community organisations such as Meals on Wheels and St Vincent de Paul. As they don’t get paid for their service, these organisations use their funds to meet the needs of the vulnerable in the community e.g. providing food for the homeless and delivering pre-cooked meals to those in need. They also present a social opportunity to those who live alone.
Aged people who are retired or phasing into retirement can provide free childcare/babysitting of grandchildren. This benefits the parents to be able to return to work and earn an income. It also benefits the grandchildren to develop a bond with their grandparents. The community also benefits with the parents contributing to the workforce and economy.
Aged people can share their knowledge with younger members of the community through volunteer mentoring programs such as Country Women’s Association and Surf Lifesaving. This instils confidence into the younger generation to take on new challenges and contribute to the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: analyses the contribution of the group through volunteering, childcare and mentoring, links each to the wider community, and gives examples of named organisations.

sampleAnswers.answer: Culturally and linguistically diverse communities bring different languages, foods and traditions to the wider community. For example, multicultural festivals invite people to share food and music from around the world, and they often draw visitors from outside the local area. Shops and restaurants that sell these foods also make them part of everyday life for many residents. Some families who settled from overseas also start small businesses, which create local jobs. Bilingual community members also help local services, such as hospitals, communicate with people who speak little English.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: sound knowledge of how the group contributes, with 'multicultural festivals invite people to share food and music' as the example, and a link to everyday community life, but the link is not explained. Explaining how such festivals bring people together and change community attitudes would lift it to the 6-7 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sole parents are part of the community and some of them need support from services.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: basic information about the group, with no contribution described. Naming one way the group contributes, with an example, would lift it to the 4-5 row.

prompts.scenario: [Category B groups, listed in two columns on the paper: Aged; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; Rural and remote families; Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Transgender, Intersex communities; Sole parents; Homeless people]
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Explore ONE example of what each group has done to try to improve community attitudes, and assess the impact this has had on the wellbeing of the group

prompts.question: Describe ONE example of how this group has attempted to improve community attitudes towards the group.
markerNotes: Choose one clear example, such as a campaign, an event or a community-run initiative, and name the group taking the action rather than listing what the group does in general.
Say how the example changes attitudes, for example by building personal contact or challenging stereotypes, not only what the example is.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a service the group receives, such as housing or health support, instead of an action taken to change community attitudes.
Giving two or more examples when the question asks for ONE, so that none is developed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Provides a sound description of ONE example of how this group has attempted to improve community attitudes towards the group
3 marks: Provides some description of ONE example of how this group has attempted to improve community attitudes towards the group
2 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of a way this group has attempted to improve community attitudes towards the group
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: The selling of ‘The Big Issue’ helps improve community attitudes towards the homeless by fostering personal connections and challenging preconceived notions. This provides a source of income for those experiencing homelessness, offering a dignified way to earn money. It also allows vendors to interact directly with the public, challenging stereotypes and fostering a sense of empathy. This interaction creates an opportunity to improve community attitudes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the sound-description row: it describes one example of how the group works to change attitudes and explains the mechanism of personal contact and challenged stereotypes.

sampleAnswers.answer: NAIDOC Week is a national celebration of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander culture and achievements, and it gives the wider community a chance to learn about them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the limited row: it names a community event that shares culture, but does not explain how the event changes attitudes towards the group. Describing the effect on people's views would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer: This group holds community events.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information only: an activity is named with no description of what it does or how it affects attitudes.

prompts.scenario:
Answer the question in relation to ONE Category B group you have studied.
Aged ; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities ; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples ; People with disabilities ; Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer, Intersex, Asexual plus (LGBTQIA+) communities ; Sole parents ; Homeless people
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Outline how community organisations advocate for each group and describe the positive influence it can have on community attitudes

prompts.question: Answer the question in relation to TWO Category B groups you have studied. Explain the benefits of community organisations advocating for the specific needs of your TWO chosen groups.
markerNotes: Explain the benefit of advocacy for each of the TWO groups, naming the specific need it addresses for each, rather than writing about advocacy in general.
Link advocacy to a change in community attitudes, such as raising awareness or promoting the rights of the group, and show how that benefits the group.
Keep the two groups distinct: a benefit explained for one group only can reach only the middle bands.
commonStudentErrors: Describing one community organisation and its services without explaining the benefit of its advocacy.
Writing about advocacy for both groups in one general paragraph, without naming the specific needs of each.
Describing the needs of the groups without the advocacy that addresses them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of the benefits of community organisations in advocating for the specific needs of the TWO chosen groups
6-7 marks: Provides a sound explanation of the benefits of community organisations in advocating for the specific needs of the TWO chosen groups
4-5 marks: Provides an explanation of the benefits of community organisations in advocating for the specific needs of the chosen group(s)
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding about advocacy and/or the role of the community organisation(s) and/or meeting specific needs of the group(s)
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Advocacy raises awareness within the community, educates the community and promotes the rights of the group.
The aged face considerable hardship, including in equitable access to services and negative community attitudes. Therefore, they benefit from advocacy organisations such as the Senior Rights Service which helps to improve public opinion and provide support. This service promotes the rights of the group by providing free legal advice and guidance on appropriate living arrangements such as residential care, promoting the safety and security needs of the group.
For the homeless, Homelessness Australia, raises awareness within the community for this group’s specific needs. By lobbying governments, they seek to improve and promote national policy which provides a voice for the homeless which improves their sense of identity. They also meet the housing needs of those children who have fled domestic violence situations, for example, providing crisis accommodation. Therefore survivors of domestic violence can be assisted with meeting an adequate standard of living.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains the benefits of advocacy for both groups, naming each group's specific needs, such as equitable access to services and housing, and links advocacy to community attitudes and policy. Both groups are developed and the answer is matched to 8 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: COTA NSW advocates for older people by raising awareness of their needs, such as access to services. This promotes their rights and can reduce negative community attitudes, so older people feel valued and more included in the community. When governments hear the case for older people's needs, such as aged care and affordable housing, they are more likely to fund services that meet those needs. Advocacy also means older people are less likely to be left out of planning for transport, housing and health in their local area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 mark row: explains the benefit of advocacy for one group, older people, linked to community attitudes and access to services. The second group is not addressed, which the 6-7 mark row requires, so a benefit for a second group would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Advocacy groups speak up for people who need help, so the community knows about their problems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 mark row: some understanding of advocacy and the role of the organisation, with no specific group, need or benefit. Naming one group and its specific need, then explaining how advocacy helps, would lift it to the 4-5 mark row.

prompts.scenario: [Category B groups, listed in two columns on the paper: Aged; Culturally and Linguistically Diverse communities; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples; Rural and remote families; Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Transgender, Intersex communities; Sole parents; Homeless people]
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Types of parents and carers (biological parents; social parents (adoption; fostering; step-parenting; surrogacy); carers (primary; informal and formal))

prompts.question: Define this type of social parent.
markerNotes: Define the type of social parent in one or two precise sentences: say what it is and what legal change or relationship makes the person a parent.
Name the legal change, such as the transfer of rights and responsibilities, rather than describing the emotional bond.
A definition states what the term means; an example or a list of features on its own does not define it.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the emotional relationship between the child and the adoptive parent, rather than the legal meaning of the term.
Naming the type of social parent without defining it.
Defining a different type of social parent, or a biological parent, instead of the one the paper names.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Provides a clear definition of the identified type of social parent
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Social parent: Adoption
Adoption is a permanent legal change where there is a transfer of the rights and responsibilities from the birth parent to the adoptive parent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: a clear definition that names the legal change, the permanent transfer of rights and responsibilities from the birth parent to the adoptive parent. The answer is brief and well matched to 2 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Adoption is when a child becomes part of another family.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about adoption, but it does not state the legal transfer of rights and responsibilities that makes it a definition. Adding that the change is permanent and legal would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.scenario: Answer parts (a)–(b) in relation to ONE type of social parent.
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Describe the different types of parents and carers

prompts.question: Describe TWO different types of carers, giving one example of each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A community health worker is writing a fact sheet for families who have recently begun caring for a relative. The fact sheet must explain the range of people who can take on a parenting or caring role.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two different types of carers accurately, with a relevant example of each
2 marks: Identifies two types of carers with some description
1 mark: Identifies one type of parent or carer
markerNotes: Give two different types of carer, such as primary and informal carers, rather than two examples of the same type.
Match each example to its type, such as a paid support worker for a formal carer, so the example shows the difference.
commonStudentErrors: Describing family roles, such as who cooks the meals, rather than the type of carer.
Giving examples without naming the type of carer each one illustrates.

sampleAnswers.answer: A primary carer is one of the parents and carers who provides most of the care for a dependant, such as a daughter who bathes, feeds and drives her father with a disability each day. An informal carer is also unpaid, usually a relative, friend or neighbour, such as a neighbour who checks on an older person and helps with shopping each week.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: two distinct types of carer, each described accurately and each with a relevant example. The answer is brief and matched to 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A primary carer provides most of the care for a dependant, such as a parent caring for a child with an illness. An informal carer is a friend who helps out without pay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: two types are identified, with some description. The informal carer has no example, so the answer does not reach full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A formal carer is a paid worker, such as a disability support worker.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: one type of carer is identified with a relevant example. A second type is needed for the second mark.

prompts.question: Distinguish between a biological parent and a social parent, using the examples in the report.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A family court report describes two households. In the first, a mother has raised her son since his birth, and in the second, a woman has become the legal parent of a child through adoption after the birth parent could not care for the child.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Distinguishes clearly between a biological parent and a social parent, using accurate examples from the report to show how the basis of each role differs
5 marks: Distinguishes between a biological parent and a social parent, using relevant examples from the report
4 marks: Distinguishes between the two types of parent with some relevant detail
3 marks: Describes both types of parent with some accuracy but little contrast between them
2 marks: Identifies one type of parent with limited description
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Contrast the basis of each role, such as birth or a legal process, rather than listing features of each parent.
Use the two households in the report to ground each type, so the difference is shown rather than asserted.
commonStudentErrors: Defining a biological parent and a social parent separately without showing how they differ.
Stating that a social parent has no legal role, when an adoptive parent holds full legal parental responsibility.

sampleAnswers.answer: A biological parent is the parent who gives birth to a child or shares their genetic material, and they hold parental rights and legal responsibility from birth. In the first household, the mother is the biological parent, and her role rests on the birth relationship she has with her son. A social parent takes on the parenting role through a legal or social process rather than through biology. In the second household, the woman is a social parent through adoption, which permanently transfers the parental rights and legal responsibility from the birth parent to her. Both parents can give love and daily care, but the key difference is the basis of the role: a biological parent's role begins with the birth, while a social parent's role is created by a legal or social arrangement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: the answer distinguishes the two types by their basis, uses both households as examples, and states the legal difference accurately.

sampleAnswers.answer: A biological parent is the child's birth parent, while a social parent becomes a parent through a legal arrangement such as adoption. The first household shows a biological parent, and the second shows an adoptive social parent who took on the role later.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: the two types are distinguished with some relevant detail. The explanation of why the difference matters is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: A social parent is an adoptive parent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: one type is identified with limited description. The answer does not contrast the two types.

dotPoints.description: Explore the impact of legal, social and technological change on social parents by considering changes in: legislation; community beliefs and attitudes; reproductive technology

prompts.question: Explain the effect of legislation OR community attitudes on this type of social parent.
markerNotes: Choose either legislation or community attitudes and explain its effect on the social parent identified in 27(a), rather than covering both in general.
Name the mechanism, such as how a change in attitudes alters the number of children available, or how legislation changes who can adopt.
Show the outcome for prospective adoptive parents, such as waiting time or choice, so that the effect is explained and not only named.
commonStudentErrors: Explaining legislation and community attitudes in general, without linking either to adoption.
Describing adoption in general, without explaining an effect of legislation or attitudes on it.
Stating an effect, such as fewer adoptions, without explaining why it happens.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of the effect of legislation OR community attitudes on the social parent identified
5 marks: Provides a sound explanation of the effect of legislation OR community attitudes on the social parent identified
4 marks: Provides an explanation of the effect of legislation OR community attitudes on the social parent identified
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of legislation and/or community attitudes and/or parent(s)
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: The number of children for adoption is reducing, making this a difficult option for prospective adoptive parents. Changing community attitudes of the acceptance of sole parents has reduced the number of children available for adoption. Government support assists single parents make the decision to remain a single parent rather than putting their child up for adoption. Additionally, community attitudes are further influenced by celebrities who have adopted children, thus encouraging people to choose this option if they are unable to have a biological child.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains the effect of changing community attitudes on adoption, linking fewer children being available, government support for sole parents and celebrity influence to prospective adoptive parents. Each influence is explained, not only named.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fewer children are available for adoption, so prospective adoptive parents may have to wait longer or consider other options. Some people may decide to try other ways of building a family instead.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 mark row: shows some understanding of an effect on adoption, that parents 'may have to wait longer', but the cause is not explained. Naming the change in community attitudes or legislation that reduces the number of children available would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Adoption is harder now than it used to be.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about adoption, with no legislation or community attitude named. Naming one influence and how it changes adoption would lift it into the 2-3 mark band.

prompts.scenario: Answer parts (a)–(b) in relation to ONE type of social parent.
prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

dotPoints.description: Examine current research data on primary carers to determine the: significance of age and gender; reasons for carers taking on the role, eg emotional obligation, alternative care too costly

prompts.question: Describe how age and gender are significant for primary carers, using the research data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A research summary of a survey of primary carers found that most respondents were women, and the largest group were aged 45 to 64. Many respondents said that they also had paid work alongside their caring role.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the significance of age and gender for primary carers, using the research data accurately and clearly to explain why each matters
3 marks: Describes age and gender for primary carers, with some use of the research data but limited explanation of significance
2 marks: Identifies a finding about age or gender from the research data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain what each finding suggests about who carries the caring role, rather than restating the figures in the summary.
Use only the findings in the summary, not general claims about carers.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the findings without explaining why age or gender matters for primary carers.

prompts.question: Examine the reasons primary carers take on the caring role, using the research data.

sampleAnswers.answer: The research data shows that emotional obligation is a major reason primary carers take on the role. A second reason is that alternative care is too costly for many households, particularly where residential facilities or formal in-home services are expensive or hard to access. Carers may therefore take on the role because it is the only realistic option, which means financial limits and personal commitment work together. These reasons also affect the carer's own wellbeing, as a strong sense of obligation can make it harder to step away from caring. The examination shows that the decision to care is shaped by relationships and by the limits of the family budget, rather than by choice alone.

This trust supports his son's emotional wellbeing and encourages him to report symptoms early. Finally, the father promotes his son's wellbeing by arranging part-time work hours that allow him to attend appointments, and by encouraging the boy to take part in a swimming activity that suits his condition. prompts.question: Evaluate the significance of each role of parents and carers for a grandparent who has become the primary carer of a teenage grandchild after a family breakdown.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A 64-year-old grandfather has become the primary carer of his 15-year-old granddaughter after her parents separated and she could no longer live at home. He is retired, has a modest pension and is learning how to support a teenager who has recently experienced upheaval.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Evaluates the significance of each role for the grandfather, making a reasoned judgement that weighs how the roles interact and which matters most in this situation
6 marks: Evaluates the significance of the roles for the grandfather, with a sound judgement supported by relevant reasons
5 marks: Evaluates some of the roles for the grandfather, with relevant reasoning but limited judgement

markerNotes: Make a judgement about which role matters most and why, rather than describing all three equally.
Link each role to the teenager's age and recent family breakdown, and to the grandfather's retirement and pension.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the roles of a parent in general without linking them to the grandfather's situation.
Concluding that one role matters most without explaining how it compares with the others.

sampleAnswers.answer: The three roles of parents and carers are each significant for this grandfather, but their significance differs because of the granddaughter's age and recent upheaval. As the primary carer, he must first satisfy specific needs. She needs a safe home, regular meals, school enrolment and health care, and a grandfather on a modest pension must plan carefully to cover these costs. Without secure basic needs, it is hard for any other role to succeed, so this role is essential even though it is practical. Building a positive relationship is arguably the most significant role for a teenager who has recently experienced separation. Trust takes time to build, and a relationship that is consistent, respectful and open to conversation gives her a secure base. This role may be harder for a grandfather who is adjusting to a new caring role and is learning to support a teenager. Promoting wellbeing draws the other two roles together. Encouraging her to keep friendships, join activities and access counselling supports her emotional, social and physical wellbeing. Overall, the relationship role carries the most weight for the granddaughter's adjustment, but it depends on her needs being met first and her wellbeing being protected. The roles are interdependent, so the grandfather's effectiveness depends on how well he balances all three.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: the significance of each role is evaluated, the roles are weighed against each other in a reasoned judgement, and the answer ties every point to the grandfather's situation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each role matters for the grandfather, but the relationship role is particularly significant for a teenager after a family breakdown. Meeting specific needs is important because she needs a safe home, but his modest pension may make this difficult.
