sampleAnswers.answer: A young carer looking after a parent can access weekly formal respite care allowing the person to attend university and sports team training sessions. This would allow the young carer to maintain their social and physical wellbeing through interaction with peers and team mates as well as the time to exercise through organised sport. Respite care for an aged carer looking after their spouse will allow time for hobbies and interests, contributing to their emotional wellbeing through time away from the demanding and time-consuming job of caring, while still ensuring the caring responsibility.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the sound-explanation row: it explains how formal respite supports the social, physical and emotional wellbeing of both a young carer and an aged carer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Respite care gives carers a break from their caring role so they can rest. A young carer might have time to see friends, and an aged carer might have time to rest.

sampleAnswers.answer: Respite care is a service that gives carers a break.

prompts.hscSection: Section I, Part B (55 marks). Attempt Questions 21–29. Allow about 1 hour and 40 minutes for this part.

prompts.question: A 16-year-old has recently begun caring for their father who has had a stroke. Assess the formal support services available to this person in preparing to become a young carer.
markerNotes: Assess means judging how useful each service would be for this young carer at the preparation stage, not only naming services.
The scenario sets a 16-year-old still at school, so the answer should weigh services for finances, health, respite and education against that situation.
Name each service and say what it provides, which gives the examples the thorough rows need.
commonStudentErrors: Listing services without judging how useful each one would be for the 16-year-old.
Describing the father’s stroke or medical care instead of the support for the young carer.
Writing about support for adult carers without relating it to a young carer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides an extensive assessment of the formal support services available to a young person preparing to become a carer; Provides relevant examples
6-7 marks: Provides a thorough assessment of the formal support services available to a young person preparing to become a carer; Provides examples
4-5 marks: Provides an understanding of the formal support services available to a young person preparing to become a carer; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Provides some information about preparations for becoming a young carer and/or support services available
1 mark: Provides relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
When preparing to become a young carer, the 16-year-old will need to organise their finances. They may access Centrelink to apply for a Carer Allowance. This would be beneficial as it allows them to pay bills to ensure an adequate standard of living for themself and their father, now that their father is no longer able to earn an income. These finances will also allow them to spend quality time with their father, rather than having a part-time job.
The young carer will also need to change their health behaviours. As a 16-year-old, their physical health would be a priority as they now need to meet the physical demands of being a carer. A community nurse may provide essential medical and education support to enhance their knowledge and skills. The carer’s physical and emotional health would be enhanced by accessing a formal support service such as Carer Gateway to find appropriate respite care, which will allow them to have time for themself with the comfort that their father is being looked after.
The carer may also need to modify the physical environment. After having a stroke, their father may need access to railings and handrails in the shower for support. They could access the Commonwealth Home Support Program (CHSP) which could provide the necessary modifications to the home. This would result in the carer having peace of mind when their father is at home by himself, while they are attending school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: assesses several formal services (financial, health and home modification) and how each would help the 16-year-old prepare, with examples of named services.

sampleAnswers.answer: A young carer can get help from Carer Gateway, which offers information and support to carers. It can also help them find respite care, so they have a break from caring. A 16-year-old preparing to care for a parent could ask Carer Gateway for information about what the caring role involves, such as helping with washing, dressing and medication, and how the family can share the work. Counselling and peer support through the service can help the young person talk about their feelings with people who understand what caring is like, which helps them manage the stress of caring. The service can also point them to other help, so they are not left to work out the system alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: shows an understanding of one formal service, Carer Gateway, through its 'help them find respite care' role and its counselling, with examples of what it helps with. Assessing how useful each service is for a 16-year-old, and naming a second service, would lift it to the 6-7 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The young carer could get support from a service such as Centrelink.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: basic information about a support service, with no assessment or link to preparing for the carer role. Naming a service and how it would help a young carer prepare would lift it to the 4-5 row.

markerNotes: Name one Act and explain how its rules create fairness or inclusion, such as stopping discrimination against people with disability, rather than naming an Act alone.

3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of how legislation can promote a just and cohesive society
2 marks: Demonstrates a limited understanding of how legislation can promote a just and cohesive society

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation that aims to promote a just and cohesive society includes the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth) (DDA). This legislation makes it illegal to discriminate against individuals based on their disability, for example, restricting an employee from a promotion based on their disability. This legislation promotes equity and aids in creating a just and fair society, as it mandates equal access, despite disability.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the sound-understanding row: it names the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth) and explains how it makes discrimination unlawful and promotes equal access. Explaining how equal access brings people together would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Anti-discrimination laws help make society fairer by stopping people being treated badly in everyday life, for example because of their disability or their background.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the limited row: it states a general purpose of anti-discrimination laws, with 'because of their disability' as an example, but names no Act and does not explain how the law works. Naming a specific Act and explaining how it makes discrimination unlawful would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation is made by parliaments.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Describe how legislation can support and protect individuals and families in contemporary society

prompts.question: Describe how ONE Australian law can support and protect individuals in contemporary society.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A woman who uses a wheelchair has applied for a job at a local business, but the entrance to the premises has steps and no ramp.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes in detail how a named law supports and protects individuals in contemporary society, with accurate and specific examples
3 marks: Describes how a named law supports or protects individuals, with some relevant detail
2 marks: Identifies a law and gives a general statement about how it protects individuals
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about legislation
markerNotes: Name one Act and then explain how its rules protect the individual in the scenario, rather than naming the Act alone.
Use the scenario to show a specific protection, such as reasonable adjustments, so that the answer applies the law.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a law without explaining how it protects anyone.
Describing what the law is about without showing how it supports individuals in contemporary society.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth) supports and protects individuals with disability in contemporary society. The legislation makes it unlawful to treat a person less favourably because of disability, including in employment, education and access to goods and services. In this situation, the business must make reasonable adjustments, such as installing a ramp, so the applicant can attend an interview and do the job. An employer cannot refuse to hire a qualified applicant simply because the premises are not accessible. By setting clear legal standards, this legislation protects individuals from discrimination and gives them a remedy if their rights are breached.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the detailed row: it names the Act, explains the unlawful treatment and applies the duty of reasonable adjustments to the scenario. Adding how a remedy would be sought would make it fuller.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 (Cth) protects people with disability from unfair treatment at work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the general row: it identifies a relevant law and makes a general statement about protection, but it does not explain how the protection works in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legislation is made by parliaments to set rules that people must follow.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about legislation, but it names no law and explains no protection for individuals.

prompts.question: Analyse how the Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) can protect the family in this situation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A mother with two primary-school children has been threatened by her former partner, who has recently waited outside the children's school. She is unsure what legal protection is available to her family.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses in detail how the Act protects the family in this situation, with accurate and specific links to the scenario
5 marks: Analyses how the Act protects the family, with sound links between its provisions and the scenario
4 marks: Analyses some ways the Act protects the family, with some links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes an aspect of the Act that has some relevance to the family's situation
2 marks: Identifies the Act and gives a general statement about protection for families
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about legislation
markerNotes: Name the order available under the Act and apply it to the children as well as the mother.
Link each protection to the scenario, such as the school, rather than describing the Act in general terms.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the Act without applying it to the family in the scenario.
Stating that the family is protected without explaining how the order works or who enforces it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) allows a court to make an apprehended domestic violence order that protects individuals and families from violence, threats and stalking. In this situation, the mother can apply for an order that stops the former partner from contacting her and the children, and from approaching their home or school. The legislation recognises that children are affected by family violence, so the order can cover them as well as the mother. This supports the family's safety and wellbeing by giving them a legal remedy that does not require them to wait for an assault. The order is enforceable by police, and a breach is a criminal offence, so the former partner faces consequences if they wait outside the school again. The mother may also need support from community services to complete the application and to help the children feel secure. Overall, the Act protects this family by providing a fast, enforceable legal remedy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the detailed row: it applies the order to the children and the school, explains enforcement and links the protection to the family's wellbeing. A brief note on the limits of the order would make the evaluation stronger.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mother can apply for an apprehended domestic violence order, which stops her former partner from contacting her and her children. Police can enforce the order if it is breached.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses some ways the Act protects the family, with links to the scenario. It does not explain how the school is covered or what the family's wider needs are.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Crimes (Domestic and Personal Violence) Act 2007 (NSW) protects people from domestic violence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the Act with a general statement about protection. It is not applied to the family or the children in the scenario.

dotPoints.description: Role of community organisations and agencies (how community organisations support government legislation and initiatives)

prompts.question: Describe how ONE community organisation supports a government initiative for families in contemporary Australia.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government announces funding for local organisations to run family support programs in regional towns.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes in detail how a named community organisation puts a government initiative into practice, with specific and accurate examples
3 marks: Describes how a community organisation supports a government initiative, with some relevant detail
2 marks: Identifies a community organisation and gives a general statement about its support for a government initiative
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about government initiatives
markerNotes: Explain the link between the government initiative and the organisation's role, such as acting as a registered provider.
Use a named initiative accurately, then describe the services the organisation delivers under it.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a community organisation without linking it to a government initiative.
Confusing government agencies with community organisations.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations and agencies help put government legislation and initiatives into practice in local areas. For example, the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), established under the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth), gives people with disability choice over their supports. Registered community organisations deliver the services funded under the scheme, such as respite care, transport and employment support, so families receive support close to home. This partnership ensures the initiative reaches the people it is designed to help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the detailed row: it names the initiative accurately and explains how community organisations deliver its services. Naming one specific family-focused outcome would sharpen it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations deliver services that the government funds, such as disability support, which helps people with disability.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a community organisation with a general statement about support. It does not name the initiative or explain how the organisation's role links to it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations are groups that help people in their local area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about community organisations, but it names no initiative and explains no government link.

prompts.question: Assess how effectively community organisations can help the government achieve the aims of this initiative.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government funds community organisations to deliver a program that helps young people at risk of homelessness find stable housing and training. Some organisations say the funding does not cover their costs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses in detail how effectively community organisations can support this initiative, weighing strengths and limitations with accurate and specific reasons
5 marks: Assesses how effectively community organisations support this initiative, with sound reasons for both strengths and limitations
4 marks: Analyses some ways community organisations support the initiative, with some reference to limitations
3 marks: Describes a role that community organisations play in the initiative, with some relevance to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a role of community organisations with a general statement about support
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about community organisations
markerNotes: Make a judgement on effectiveness, not just a list of what organisations do.
Use the funding concern in the scenario as a limitation and discuss how it affects the aims of the initiative.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the roles of community organisations without making a judgement on how effective they are.
Ignoring the funding issue in the scenario when assessing effectiveness.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations can be effective partners in this initiative because they have local knowledge and existing trust with young people. They can reach young people who avoid government agencies, and they can provide housing referrals, case management and emotional support. Their effectiveness, however, depends on adequate funding, since grants that do not cover staff wages and rent may limit how many young people they can help. Community organisations also need clear reporting requirements so the government can measure outcomes and check that the initiative is meeting its aims. Coordination between agencies is important because a young person may need housing, health and education support at the same time. Overall, community organisations help government legislation and initiatives succeed when they are adequately funded and work in partnership with agencies, but their impact is limited when funding does not reflect the real cost of their services.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the detailed row: it weighs strengths and limitations and reaches a judgement linked to the funding concern. Addressing a counter-argument about government accountability would strengthen it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations can reach young people who avoid government agencies, and they can provide support such as housing referrals. However, if the funding does not cover staff and rent, they may not be able to help as many young people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses some ways organisations support the initiative and refers to the funding limitation. It does not reach a clear overall judgement on effectiveness.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations can help the government by giving young people support with housing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one role with a general statement. It makes no judgement about effectiveness and does not use the scenario's funding concern.

dotPoints.description: Explore how community organisations and agencies interact with governments to support and protect individuals and families in contemporary society

prompts.question: Evaluate how effectively community organisations implement government legislation and initiatives for individuals and families in contemporary society.
markerNotes: Evaluate means judging how effectively: name a strength and a limitation for each organisation or law, then say what the difference means for families’ wellbeing.
The top rows reward a clear judgement backed by named legislation and organisations, such as the Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) and women’s refuges.
Link each point to wellbeing, such as safety, financial security or emotional health, and keep the argument logical from one paragraph to the next.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what community organisations do without judging how effectively they put the legislation into practice.
Naming legislation without linking it to a specific organisation or to how families are affected.
Making a one-sided judgement, such as calling organisations effective, with no limitation such as funding or waiting lists.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding of community organisations, government legislation and initiatives in contemporary society; Provides clear and valid evaluation about how community organisations effectively implement government legislation and initiatives for individuals and families; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of individuals and families; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive answer
10-12 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of community organisations, government legislation and initiatives in contemporary society; Provides some evaluation about how community organisations effectively implement government legislation and initiatives for individuals and families; Provides a link(s) to the effect on the wellbeing of individuals and families; Communicates information using relevant examples; Presents a cohesive answer
7-9 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of community organisations, government legislation and initiatives in contemporary society; Provides a link to how community organisations effectively implement government legislation and initiatives for individuals and/or families; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Provides basic information of community organisations and/or government legislation and/or initiatives for individuals and/or families in a contemporary society; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about community organisations and/or government legislation and/or initiatives and/or individuals and/or families in a contemporary society

sampleAnswers.answer:
Community organisations are the main way that government legislation and initiatives reach individuals and families in everyday life. Their effectiveness is strongest where they are well funded and close to the people they serve, but their reach is uneven, and because they rely heavily on government grants, the quality of support varies between services and between communities.

The clearest example of effective implementation is family violence support. The Family Law Act 1975 (Cth) allows courts to make orders that protect people from family violence, and women’s refuges help women and their children to apply for those orders, find safe accommodation and rebuild their lives. Here the law becomes practical safety, which has a direct and positive effect on the physical and emotional wellbeing of women and children. Relationships Australia shows a similar pattern in family law, where its family dispute resolution services help separating parents reach parenting arrangements without going to court, which reduces conflict and supports children’s relationships with both parents.

Organisations also turn anti-discrimination law into everyday protection. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) prohibits discrimination on grounds such as sex, race and disability, but a law on its own does not change attitudes. Community groups that support families of LGBTIQA+ people, such as PFLAG, provide information and support that helps families accept and include their members, which protects individuals who might otherwise face isolation. Advocacy by community groups also helped bring about the 2017 change to the Marriage Act that allowed same-sex couples to marry, showing that lobbying can change legislation itself.

However, the effectiveness of these organisations is limited in several ways. Many rely on short-term government funding, which makes it hard to plan services and keep experienced staff, so waiting lists form for crisis services such as refuges and counselling. Families in rural and remote areas may have few services at all, so legislation that applies to them in principle may not help them in practice. People with low literacy or limited English may also struggle to find or use the services they are entitled to. These gaps mean that the wellbeing benefits of the law are unevenly shared.

On balance, community organisations implement government legislation and initiatives effectively in crisis and legal support, where their work is clearly linked to safety and legal rights. They are less effective where funding is insecure, where demand exceeds capacity and in regional areas. The most effective approach is one where government funding is stable and organisations work together, so that a family can move from legal advice to counselling to housing without being turned away at each step.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: judges how effectively organisations put the Family Law Act and anti-discrimination law into practice, weighs strengths against limits such as funding and unmet demand, and links each judgement to the wellbeing of individuals and families. The overall judgement follows from the discussion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations such as women's refuges and Relationships Australia put laws like the Family Law Act into practice. They help people get protection and support families through separation. A refuge, for example, can help a woman and her children find safe accommodation while she works through the legal steps available to her, such as applying for a protection order. Relationships Australia offers counselling and family dispute resolution, so parents can reach agreements about their children without going straight to court. Government funding helps these services to run, and each organisation decides how to spend it in its own area. Many of these organisations also rely on volunteers and donations alongside government funding, which can make their services harder to plan for. However, they do not always have enough staff, so some people have to wait for help. A family in a rural town may have to travel a long way to reach a counsellor, while a family in a city may have more services to choose from. Access therefore depends partly on where people live, as well as on the law itself, and this affects the wellbeing of the individuals and families who need help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of how organisations 'put laws like the Family Law Act into practice', with examples of refuges and Relationships Australia, and a note of one limit, staff shortages. Judging how effective the organisations are, with a clear link to wellbeing, would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Community organisations help families, and the government makes laws to protect them, such as the Family Law Act.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: relevant information about organisations and legislation, with no evaluation and no example of effectiveness. Describing how one organisation puts one law into practice, and whether it works, would lift it to the 4-6 row.

dotPoints.description: The government’s role (legislation relating to the protection and welfare of children (child protection; education, eg school attendance; safety, eg travel restraints, product safety standards); government agencies that implement and monitor these laws, eg NSW Commission for Children and Young People)

prompts.question: Explain how travel restraint legislation and government agencies protect the welfare of children when travelling in a vehicle. Provide examples to support your answer.
markerNotes: Name the legislation, such as the Road Rules 2014, and at least one government agency, then explain what each does to protect children travelling by car.
Make the examples specific: the type of restraint for each age or size, rather than the general statement that children must be restrained.
Explain why the law protects the child, such as why a rearward-facing restraint protects an infant in a crash.
commonStudentErrors: Describing car seats without naming any legislation or government agency.
Naming an agency without explaining what it does to protect children when travelling.
Describing general road rules that apply to all passengers instead of the protection of children.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Provides a thorough explanation about travel restraint law(s) and government agencies that protect the welfare of children when travelling in a vehicle; Provides relevant examples
6 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding about travel restraint law(s) and government agencies that protect the welfare of children when travelling in a vehicle; Provides some relevant examples
4-5 marks: Demonstrates some understanding about travel restraint law and/or government agencies that protect the welfare of children when travelling in a vehicle; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Provides some information about travel restraints and/or government agencies
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
All children must be safely fastened in the correct child car seat for their age and size/weight. This ensures that children are as physically safe as possible in road vehicles and are less likely to be injured/killed in the event of a car crash.
Rule 266 of Road Rules 2014 addresses the regulation of the wearing of seat belts. Eg a child up to 6 months should be secured in an approved rearward facing restraint, a child from 6 months to 4 years to be secured in rear/forward facing child restraint with inbuilt harness and a child from 7 years to 16 years may have a booster seat.
The Child Restraint Evaluation Program and the Authorised Restraint Fitting Stations are other NSW Government initiatives to offer support.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains the rules on child restraints and how each restraint fits the child age and size, with examples and the protective purpose of each. It also names government initiatives that support families.

sampleAnswers.answer: Children must use a child car seat that suits their age and size. For example, a baby is placed in a rearward facing restraint, which helps protect the head and neck in a crash. Older children move to a booster seat once they have outgrown the harness, so the adult seat belt sits correctly across the hips and chest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: some understanding, with examples of a 'rearward facing restraint' and a booster seat, but no legislation or agency is named. Naming the Road Rules 2014 and one agency, and explaining their role, would lift it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council should prioritise upgrading the swimming pool's fencing and supervision because drowning is a severe and irreversible risk for young children. Playground upgrades also protect children, but their injuries are usually less severe than drowning and can often be reduced through routine repairs. Upgrading the fencing addresses a specific hazard that affects children across the local community, not only those who use the park. Prioritising the pool also supports families by reducing the risk that children enter water without supervision, which protects the welfare of every child in the household. Therefore, the council's limited budget is best directed to the swimming pool provision, while the playground is maintained through routine repairs.

subTopics.name: Assisting young people to become young adults

dotPoints.description: The government’s role in regulating rights of young people (licensing drivers; school attendance; access to tobacco and alcohol; gambling regulations; right to vote; legal age for sexual relationships and marriage)

prompts.question:
Assess the effectiveness of the government in regulating the rights of young people. In your answer, refer to:
• licensing drivers
• school attendance
• access to tobacco and alcohol
markerNotes: Judge the effectiveness of the government's regulation in each of the three areas, then reach a verdict on the whole; a list of laws without a verdict stays in the lower bands.
Link each regulation to the wellbeing of young people, such as safety, health, education or future employment, rather than only to the law.
Name a limitation for each measure, such as its reliance on compliance or on family support, so that the assessment is balanced.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the laws for each area without judging how effective they are.
Writing about the rights of young people in general, rather than the government's regulation of licensing, school attendance and tobacco and alcohol.
Giving a verdict with no evidence, such as saying the laws are effective without showing how they affect young people.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Provides an extensive assessment of the effectiveness of the government in regulating licensing drivers, school attendance and access to tobacco and alcohol; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of young people; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive response
10-12 marks: Provides a thorough assessment of the effectiveness of the government in regulating licensing drivers, school attendance and access to tobacco and alcohol; Provides link(s) to the effect on the wellbeing of young people; Communicates information using relevant examples; Presents a cohesive response
7-9 marks: Provides an assessment of the effectiveness of the government in regulating licensing drivers, school attendance and/or access to tobacco and alcohol; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of the government’s role in regulating the rights of young people; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about the rights of young people and/or the role of government

sampleAnswers.answer:
The government has been largely effective in regulating the rights of young people. Its laws protect young people from serious harm while still letting them gain independence step by step, and the measures are strongest where the rules are clear, enforced and linked to a clear outcome. The three areas of licensing drivers, school attendance and access to tobacco and alcohol show both the strengths and the limits of this approach.

Licensing drivers is the clearest success. The Graduated Licensing Scheme in NSW lets young people build experience over several provisional stages, with restrictions that reduce the risks new drivers face. This protects young drivers and other road users from serious injury, and it supports wellbeing because a young person who avoids a crash keeps their health, independence and the chance to study or work. Its limitation is that the restrictions depend on compliance, so a young driver who ignores them can still put others at risk.

School attendance laws require children to attend school from six years of age until they complete Year 10, and then to be in school, approved training or full-time paid work, or a combination, until they turn 17. This supports wellbeing because education builds the skills for employment, social connections with peers and an understanding of rights and responsibilities. However, compulsory attendance does not guarantee learning. A young person who attends but disengages, or whose family does not enforce the law, may gain little. The effectiveness of the rule therefore depends on schools and families offering support, such as welfare staff who identify students at risk of leaving early.

Access to tobacco and alcohol is regulated by making it illegal to sell or supply alcohol to people under 18, by preventing minors from being in licensed premises unless accompanied by an adult, and by banning the sale of tobacco to people under 18. These rules make the substances harder to obtain, which reduces the early harm to young people's health. The limitation is that many young people obtain alcohol and tobacco from friends or older people, so the rules cannot stop every supply. Enforcement, including penalties for adults who buy for minors, is therefore essential to their effectiveness.

Overall, the government's regulation is effective in reducing the most serious risks, especially on the road and in access to harmful substances, where the rules are clear and enforced. The regulation of school attendance is effective in principle but depends on support beyond the law. The three measures share a weakness: age limits and minimum standards cannot change the attitudes that lead some young people to test those limits. Their effect on wellbeing is therefore strongest when they are combined with education and community support. On balance, the government's approach is effective, but not complete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: an extensive assessment of the government's regulation of licensing drivers, school attendance and access to tobacco and alcohol, with a verdict on the whole and clear links to young people's wellbeing. The limits of each measure keep the verdict qualified, which is what separates it from the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government has been largely effective in regulating the rights of young people. Its laws protect young people from serious harm while still letting them gain independence step by step. The three areas of licensing drivers, school attendance and access to tobacco and alcohol show both the strengths and the limits of this approach. Licensing drivers is the clearest success. The graduated licensing scheme in NSW lets young people build experience over several provisional stages, with restrictions that reduce the risks new drivers face. This protects young drivers and other road users, which supports young people's wellbeing. School attendance laws keep young people in education, which supports their future work and social connections. However, the law is only as strong as the support a young person receives at school, and a student who is struggling may still stop attending. Access to tobacco and alcohol is the weakest of the three areas. Age limits make these substances harder to get, but some young people still obtain them from friends or older people, so these rules are only partly effective at protecting wellbeing. Overall, the government does well where the law is clear and enforced, but the wellbeing gains depend on support beyond the law, such as family and community programs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: an assessment of how effective government action is across the three areas, with examples such as the graduated licensing scheme, and 'the weakest of the three areas' for tobacco and alcohol. The verdict is brief and the link to wellbeing is general, so judging one measure more closely against the wellbeing of young people would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The law restricts the rights of young people on provisional licences, for example through a zero blood alcohol limit and limits on carrying passengers. These restrictions reflect the age appropriateness of driving rights, because young drivers have less experience in identifying and responding to hazards and face a higher risk of crashes. The restrictions protect the young driver and other road users while allowing the young person to gain experience and move towards full rights. In the scenario, the rules may limit how many friends can ride with the 17-year-old, especially late at night.

prompts.question: Discuss whether the minimum age for buying alcohol should be raised, considering the age appropriateness of the rights young people are given.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A community forum is debating whether 17-year-olds should be allowed to hold a full driving licence without restrictions, and whether the minimum age for buying alcohol should be raised from 18.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses in detail whether the minimum age should be raised, with a balanced argument on both sides and a reasoned conclusion
5 marks: Discusses the minimum age with sound arguments on both sides, reaching a supported conclusion
4 marks: Discusses some arguments about the minimum age and the rights young people are given, with a limited conclusion

markerNotes: Present arguments on both sides, such as brain development and harm reduction, before reaching a conclusion.

commonStudentErrors: Giving a personal opinion without weighing arguments on both sides.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people's rights should reflect their developing maturity, but the age appropriateness of each right is debated. The case for keeping the current minimum age of 18 for buying alcohol is that the minimum age sets a clear legal line and reflects a view that young people are still developing judgement. The case for raising it is that alcohol-related harm can affect young people's health and safety. However, raising the minimum age may not address harm if young people obtain alcohol from others, so education and enforcement matter too. For the 17-year-old drivers in the scenario, graduated restrictions suggest that the law already treats driving rights as earned through experience. Overall, the law's current approach is largely appropriate, but the debate would benefit from stronger evidence about where young people's risk is greatest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the detailed row: it presents arguments on both sides, considers an alternative approach and reaches a reasoned conclusion. Stating more precisely which evidence would settle the debate would strengthen it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Raising the minimum age for alcohol would protect young people's health, but it may not stop them obtaining alcohol from others. Driving restrictions suggest the law sees rights as age-related, so the same reasoning may apply.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses some arguments and refers to the age appropriateness of rights. The conclusion is limited and the case for keeping the current age is not developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: A passport is an entitlement that young people can obtain once they meet the identity requirements under the Passports Act 2005 (Cth). It allows them to travel overseas, to access consular assistance and to meet entry requirements in other countries. Workplace protections are another entitlement, and the national minimum wage sets the lowest pay rate that employers must provide to employees under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). This helps ensure that young workers receive a fair minimum rate for their work. Together, these entitlements support the independence of young people as they move into adult life.

sampleAnswers.answer: The entitlements in this scenario support the young person's transition to adulthood in practical ways. The workplace protections, including the national minimum wage under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), ensure the café job pays a lawful minimum rate and that the young person's work is valued. However, the benefits depend on the young person knowing their rights, because young people who do not understand the minimum wage may accept less pay. Similarly, a passport does not protect the traveller from their own poor decisions. Overall, the entitlements support the transition well, but their effectiveness depends on the young person's knowledge and the support their parents provide.

dotPoints.description: Examine differing societal expectations of young females and young males as they assume increasing rights, responsibilities and opportunities

prompts.question: Analyse how societal expectations affect young people as they assume more rights and responsibilities.
markerNotes: Analyse rather than list: for each area, say what the expectation is, why society holds it and how it changes what a young person can do or feel.
Link each example to the wellbeing of young people, such as financial wellbeing, school engagement or self-esteem; a link stated once at the end is not enough.
Develop two or three examples fully, such as driving, part-time work or voting, rather than naming many.
commonStudentErrors: Listing rights, such as driving or voting, without naming the expectation that comes with them.
Stating that expectations affect wellbeing without saying how.
Treating all young people as one group where the expectations for young females and young males differ.
keywords: expectations of young females and males
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Provides an extensive analysis of the affect societal expectations has on young people as they assume more rights and responsibilities; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of young people; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive response
10-12 marks: Provides a thorough analysis of the affect societal expectations has on young people as they assume more rights and responsibilities; Provides link(s) to the effect on the wellbeing of young people; Communicates information using relevant examples; Presents a cohesive response
7-9 marks: Provides an analysis of the affect societal expectations has on young people as they assume more rights and responsibilities; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of societal expectations on young people as they assume more rights and responsibilities; Provide example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about societal expectations on young people and/or rights and responsibilities when becoming an adult

sampleAnswers.answer:
Societal expectations shape how young people experience the rights and responsibilities that come with growing up, and they affect wellbeing as much as the law does. Expectations about when a young person is ready for adult responsibilities can open or close opportunities, and they often differ for young women and young men. The effect is clearest in three areas: driving, school and work, and access to adult activities such as alcohol and voting.

Driving shows how expectations and rights meet. In NSW a young person moves through the graduated licensing scheme, gaining a licence in stages, and the rights grow as the young driver shows they can manage the risk. Yet society also expects young drivers to be careless, and this expectation is reflected in higher insurance premiums, especially for young males. The expectation can encourage caution, but it also adds to the cost of a right that many young people need for work and study, so it affects their financial wellbeing and their independence.

School and paid work bring a different set of expectations. Society expects young people to attend school and achieve, while also expecting them to take on part-time jobs and build a work history. These expectations can conflict. A part-time job that runs late may cause fatigue, which can reduce school attendance and engagement. Young people who leave traditional schooling are often judged negatively, even when they are training or working in a sound alternative pathway. That judgement can damage self-esteem and make it harder for young people to ask for help when they need it, which affects their emotional wellbeing.

Access to tobacco and alcohol at 18 and the right to vote carry expectations too. The law sets 18 as the age for buying alcohol and tobacco, and the community expects young adults to behave responsibly once they can do so. When young people experiment with drugs or alcohol, however, the wider community often labels them as troublemakers, which can lead to exclusion from social spaces and reduce the support they receive. The right to vote is different. It assumes that young people will understand government policy and make informed decisions, which encourages civic participation, but it also assumes a level of political knowledge that not every young person has been taught.

Overall, societal expectations affect young people in both positive and negative ways. They encourage responsibility and build capability, but they can also restrict choices when the expectation is stereotyped or unrealistic. The most damaging effects arise when rights and expectations do not match, for example when a young person is expected to carry adult responsibilities at work but is still treated as a child in family decisions. Expectations therefore affect wellbeing most strongly when they shape access to rights in practice, not only when the law grants those rights.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: it analyses how driving, school and work, and access to adult activities carry societal expectations, links each to young people's wellbeing, and uses examples throughout. A firmer judgement on which expectation matters most would lift the answer further.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Societal expectations affect young people as they gain rights, because the community expects them to act responsibly once they have those rights. Driving is one example. Young people in NSW gain a licence in stages, and insurance costs are higher for young males, which reflects an expectation that they will be less careful. This affects their wellbeing because the cost limits how far they can use the right to work or study.

School and work also matter. Young people who take on part-time work may find their attendance falls, and young people who leave school early are often seen negatively. These expectations shape how young people feel about themselves.

Access to alcohol and tobacco at 18 and the right to vote also carry expectations. Young people who experiment with drugs or alcohol are often seen as troublemakers, which affects their reputation with others in the community. Overall, societal expectations shape how young people use their rights, and this can affect wellbeing in positive and negative ways.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: it analyses expectations around driving and school with examples, but the links to wellbeing are brief and the examples are less developed than in a top answer. Developing the wellbeing link for each example would move it into the 10–12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people gain rights such as driving, voting and buying alcohol as they get older. Society expects them to take on responsibilities, such as driving safely and attending school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: it describes rights and responsibilities but does not analyse how societal expectations affect young people. Choosing one expectation and explaining its effect on wellbeing would move it up.

markerNotes: Judge the extent: say how far legislation and entitlements address current issues, name the issues they miss, and reach a position. A list of Acts without a verdict stays in the lower bands.

Choose two or three current issues, such as housing needs or access to in-home care, and say exactly what each measure does about them.
commonStudentErrors: Describing legislation and entitlements without a judgement on how far they address current issues.
Listing Acts and payments without naming the current issue each one responds to.
Writing about the aged as one group without linking any measure to their wellbeing.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding about the relationship between current issues and government legislation and entitlements; Provides a well-informed judgement on the extent to which current issues support the aged; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of individuals; Presents a logical and cohesive response using relevant examples
10-12 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding about the relationship between current issues and government legislation and entitlements; Provides a judgement on the extent to which current issues support the aged; Provides links to the effect on the wellbeing of individuals; Presents a cohesive response using relevant examples
7-9 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge about the relationship between current issues and government legislation and entitlements; Provides a link(s) between current issues and the aged; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Provides some information about current issues and/or government legislation and/or entitlements and/or the aged; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Government legislation and entitlements address many current issues for older people, but they do not resolve them all. Their main strength is that they set out the rights of the aged and provide income and in-home support. Their limitation is that they respond unevenly to issues that law cannot easily solve, such as housing costs and social isolation, so some older people's wellbeing is still at risk.

The Aged Care Act 2024 places the rights of older people at the centre of the aged care system. It aims to make the system simpler, with supported decision making, so that services are safe and of high quality. This responds to the serious failings identified by the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety, whose final report in 2021 called for major change. The Act improves wellbeing by setting clear standards, but a standard on paper does not guarantee a suitable place in a facility for every older person who needs one.

Many older people prefer to remain in their own homes, and the Support at Home Program is designed to help them do this. It can fund specialist services and home modifications, which allows an older person to stay healthy, happy and safe at home for longer. This addresses the issue of independence directly. Its effect depends on the availability of workers and on the older person's ability to navigate the system, so people with limited digital skills or family support may gain less from it.

The Age Discrimination Act 2004 makes it unlawful to treat a person unfairly because of their age, which targets ageism in employment, services and the community. This protects the wellbeing of older people who want to keep working or take part in community life. However, the law relies on individuals making complaints, and many older people may not do so, particularly if they depend on the person they would complain about.

Government entitlements, especially the Age Pension, reduce financial hardship. For many older people the pension is a main source of income, and it helps with the costs of housing, food and health care. It supports wellbeing by reducing financial stress. Yet the pension does not solve the housing affordability problem that many older renters face, and no entitlement can by itself prevent loneliness or social isolation.

Overall, government legislation and entitlements address current issues for the aged to a considerable extent, because they protect rights, support independent living and provide income. They do less well on issues such as housing costs and social isolation, which have a direct effect on wellbeing but depend on communities and families as much as on law. The extent of their success therefore depends on whether the services that legislation promises are actually delivered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: extensive knowledge of the Aged Care Act 2024, the Support at Home Program, the Age Discrimination Act and the Age Pension, a judgement on the extent to which they address current issues, and clear links to wellbeing. The verdict is qualified by what the measures cannot do, which keeps it well informed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Government legislation and entitlements address some current issues for the aged. The Aged Care Act 2024 puts the rights of older people at the centre of care and aims to make services safe and of high quality, which supports their wellbeing. Older people who receive care that respects their choices are more likely to feel in control of their daily lives. The Age Pension gives older people an income, which helps them meet everyday costs such as food, medicines and power bills, so they are less likely to go without essentials. The Age Discrimination Act 2004 also protects older people from unfair treatment because of age, such as being refused a job or a service only because of their age, which protects their dignity and their sense of being valued. Support at Home helps older people stay in their own homes, so they can remain independent for longer and keep the social ties of their own neighbourhood. However, many older people still struggle with housing costs, and the legislation does not directly address this. A pensioner renting in an expensive area may have little left after rent, so an income payment alone does not solve the problem of finding secure housing. Loneliness is another issue that a payment cannot fix, because it depends on social contact and community connection rather than money. Overall, legislation and entitlements help the aged to some extent, but they do not address every current issue.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of how the Act, the pension, the Age Discrimination Act and Support at Home relate to current issues, with examples, and 'a payment cannot fix' for loneliness. The verdict is stated in one sentence rather than argued, and the link to wellbeing is brief. Weighing the verdict against the housing and isolation gaps, with the wellbeing effect of each, would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government has laws about aged care, and older people get the Age Pension. These help older people with money and care, but some older people still have problems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: some relevant information about legislation and entitlements, with no judgement and no link to the issues the question names. Naming one current issue and one measure that responds to it would lift it to the 4-6 row.

prompts.scenario:
Your answer will be assessed on how well you:
• demonstrate knowledge and understanding of societal influences on wellbeing relevant to the question
• apply the skills of critical thinking and analysis
• communicate ideas and information using relevant examples
• present a logical and cohesive response
prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a case study on the aged by considering the following questions: what are the current and future issues for the aged?; how do government entitlements assist the aged in planning for retirement?; what is available in the community to support the housing needs of the aged?; how can the community recognise the aged as valuable citizens?

prompts.question: Explain how the housing needs of the aged can be assisted by community support services.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism for each support, such as a home modification that lets an older person stay independent, rather than naming the service.
Name at least one real support program or organisation and what it provides, so the examples are specific.
Cover more than one housing option, such as staying at home, moving to a retirement village or residential care, to show the range of needs.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the housing needs of older people without naming any community support service.
Naming a service but not explaining how it helps with housing.
Treating government pensions as community support services without explaining their link to housing.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding about how the housing needs of the aged can be assisted by community support services; Provides a thorough explanation of how the housing needs of the aged can be assisted by community support services; Provides relevant examples
4-5 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding about how the housing needs of the aged can be assisted by community support services; Provides a sound explanation of how the housing needs of the aged can be assisted by community support services; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Provides some information about community support for the aged and/or the housing needs of the aged
1 mark: Provides relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Aged people can reside in their own home, downsize to smaller accommodation such as a villa, move to a retirement village or move to an aged care facility. Support within the community can be provided by organisations such as Aged and Community Services Australia (ACSA), Assistance with Care and Housing for the Aged (ACHA) and Commonwealth Homes Support Program (CHSP) which can assist aged individuals with this transition when required.
ACSA provide quality, affordable housing and care services which support older Australians. This allows capable individuals to remain in their own home living independently or in a retirement village. ACHA supports lower income aged individuals by providing subsidised housing. This then allows aged people to meet their other financial commitments. CHSP provide modifications to the home such as ramps and railings to promote independent living. This will result in individuals being able to remain in their own home for longer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains several housing options and the community organisations and programs that help with each, and why each helps the aged stay independent.

sampleAnswers.answer: Older people may want to stay in their own home. Community services can help them by providing home modifications, such as grab rails and ramps, so they can keep living there safely. Without these changes, a person with reduced mobility may be at risk of falls, which can force a move into residential care before they need one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some information about one community support, 'providing home modifications', with a brief example, but the explanation of how it helps is limited. Naming a second option and explaining its effect on independence would lift it to the 4-5 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some older people need a place to live.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: relevant information about the housing needs of older people, with no community support named. Naming one support service would lift it to the 2-3 row.

dotPoints.description: Technology as hardware, eg appliances, gadgets, toys; technology as software, eg applications, databases, websites; technology as organisation of knowledge, eg communications, media, internet, home entertainment

prompts.question: How can complex technologies assist in the organisation of knowledge?
markerNotes: Name a complex technology, such as a smartphone, and explain how its apps or software collate and organise information so that it can be found.
Show the benefit to the user, such as faster access to information or automatic sorting, rather than listing features.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a complex technology's features without saying how it organises knowledge.
Using a primitive technology, such as paper or books, as the example.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of how complex technologies can assist in the organisation of knowledge
3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of how complex technologies assist in the organisation of knowledge
2 marks: Demonstrates a limited understanding of how complex technologies assist in the organisation of knowledge
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Complex technologies such as mobile phones have apps that can collate all information such as contacts, photos, calendars and emails in one place which allows for fast access to information. Technology has been developed in a way to become intuitive when gaining data, for example, mobile phones can automatically collate pictures and create presentations of memories based on events or locations.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the sound-understanding row: it names mobile phones and explains how apps collate contacts, photos and calendars for fast access, with an example of automatic sorting. Explaining how this changes the way people find or share knowledge would strengthen it.

sampleAnswers.answer: An individual could store contacts, photos and calendars on a mobile phone in one place, so that they can find them quickly when needed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the limited row: it names a complex technology, and 'store contacts, photos and calendars', with a reason, but does not explain how the technology organises knowledge across sources. Explaining how the apps sort or link information would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mobile phones are used by many people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information only: no link to how the technology organises knowledge.
