dotPoints.description: Technologies and the workplace (safety technology; information and communication technology; structure of the workplace (health and safety; equipment; efficiency; flexibility; education and training); introduction of technology into the workplace)

prompts.question: Outline TWO ways safety technology can improve health and safety in a warehouse workplace.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A warehouse is introducing new equipment after several near-miss incidents between forklifts and pedestrians. Management is considering proximity sensors on forklifts and fall-detection devices worn by staff.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines two ways safety technology improves health and safety, with accurate examples from the warehouse
2 marks: Outlines one way safety technology improves health and safety, with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about safety technology in the workplace
markerNotes: Name each technology and state what it does to protect workers, rather than listing devices.
Link the technology to the scenario, such as forklifts and pedestrians, to show accuracy.
Stating that technology is good for safety without an outline stays at 1 mark.
commonStudentErrors: Naming safety technology without explaining how it improves health and safety.
Describing cost or staff training rather than safety.
Giving two examples that are the same device.

sampleAnswers.answer: Proximity sensors on forklifts alert the driver when a worker is nearby, which reduces the risk of collisions in busy aisles. Fall-detection devices worn by staff can send an alert to a supervisor if a worker falls, so help can be provided quickly. Both examples of safety technology improve health and safety in the workplace by preventing injuries in the warehouse and reducing the time before assistance arrives.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two distinct ways safety technology protects workers, with accurate examples from the warehouse. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sensors on the forklift warn the driver when a worker is nearby, reducing collisions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one way safety technology improves safety, with limited detail about the effect on health.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technology makes the warehouse safer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant but general information with no outline of how a technology improves safety.

prompts.question: Analyse how introducing technology into the workplace can affect flexibility and education and training for employees.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A printing company plans to introduce cloud-based scheduling software, online training modules and automated cutting machines. Some workers are keen to learn new skills, while others worry they may lose hours if machines take over their tasks.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses thoroughly how technology can affect flexibility and education and training for employees, using specific examples and considering uneven effects on different workers
5 marks: Analyses in detail how technology can affect flexibility and education and training, using relevant examples from the scenario
4 marks: Analyses how technology affects flexibility or education and training, with some relevant examples
3 marks: Describes an effect of workplace technology on flexibility or training with limited analysis
2 marks: Identifies a workplace technology with minimal reference to flexibility or training
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about technology in the workplace
markerNotes: Analyse both effects, then show who gains and who may lose, such as workers who lose hours to automated machines.
Use the scenario's three technologies, so the answer addresses the actual workplace change.
Acknowledging that employees' confidence affects how much they benefit shows analysis at the top of the band.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the technologies without analysing their effect on flexibility or training.
Assuming all employees benefit equally from new technology.
Treating flexibility as a benefit to employees only, with no consideration of how managers may use it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Introducing technology into the workplace can increase flexibility for employees. Cloud-based scheduling software allows staff to view shifts, swap hours and sometimes work from different locations, which helps them balance work with family or study commitments. However, flexibility can be uneven. Workers who are not comfortable with the software may find it harder to manage changes, and managers may use the system to schedule people at short notice. Online training modules also affect education and training. They allow employees to learn new skills at their own pace, and the company can train many people without taking them off the floor for long. Keen workers may therefore gain more skills and career options. Yet those who are less confident with online learning may fall behind, and automated cutting machines may reduce the hours of workers whose tasks are replaced. Overall, technology can increase flexibility and training opportunities, but its effects depend on how the workplace supports employees.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the effects on flexibility and on education and training, and considers who gains and who may lose. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cloud scheduling software can give employees more flexibility, because staff can view and swap shifts. Online training modules let employees learn new skills at their own pace. However, workers who lose hours to automated machines may not benefit from either change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses how two technologies affect flexibility and training, with examples from the scenario, but the uneven effects on workers are only briefly considered.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scheduling software and training modules are new technologies in the workplace.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two workplace technologies with minimal reference to flexibility or training.

dotPoints.description: Assess the degree to which technology impacts on: workplace safety; work/life balance; career pathways

prompts.question: Describe how technology can affect workplace safety for employees in a warehouse.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional warehouse has replaced most manual stock handling with automated conveyors, robotic pickers and handheld scanners. Staff now work alongside moving machinery and spend long shifts at scanning stations.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes at least two effects of technology on workplace safety, with accurate links to the warehouse
3 marks: Describes two effects of technology on workplace safety, with some links to the warehouse
2 marks: Identifies one effect of technology on workplace safety, with a limited link to the scenario
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about technology and workplace safety
markerNotes: Name each technology in the warehouse and the specific safety risk or benefit it creates, rather than general statements about safety.
Credit answers that show both sides, such as automation removing heavy lifting while introducing risk from moving machinery.
A claim that technology is good or bad for safety, with no mechanism, stays in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Saying technology always makes workplaces safer, with no explanation of how.
Describing workplace safety in general without linking it to the warehouse in the scenario.
Listing machines without explaining the safety risk or benefit each one creates.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this warehouse, automated conveyors and robotic pickers can improve workplace safety by removing the need for staff to lift heavy cartons and reach into high shelving, which lowers the risk of manual handling injuries such as back strain. Sensors on the machines can also stop them when a person enters their path. However, technology can create new risks. Staff working near moving machinery may be struck or trapped if guarding and training are inadequate, and long periods at scanning stations can cause repetitive strain injuries to the wrists and neck.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two clear effects are described, one reducing risk and one increasing it, and both are tied to the warehouse. The answer uses the key terms accurately and is concise.

sampleAnswers.answer: Automated machines can reduce heavy lifting, which helps workplace safety, but staff can still be hurt by moving machinery.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one effect of technology on workplace safety with a brief link to the warehouse. A second effect, such as repetitive strain from scanning, would move it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technology can make work safer but it can also be dangerous.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about technology and safety, but does not identify a specific effect in the warehouse.

prompts.question: Assess the degree to which technology impacts on work/life balance and career pathways for Ravi.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Ravi works as a technician for a national telecommunications company. Since the company introduced a cloud-based messaging app, he receives work messages at night and on weekends. The company has also offered him training in data analysis, which could lead to a new role.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a thorough assessment of the degree to which technology impacts on Ravi's work/life balance and career pathways, reaching a justified judgement
5 marks: Provides a sound assessment of the degree to which technology impacts on work/life balance and career pathways, with clear links to Ravi
4 marks: Provides an assessment of technology's impact on work/life balance and career pathways, with some judgement
3 marks: Describes technology's impact on work/life balance or career pathways, with limited assessment of its degree
2 marks: Identifies an effect of technology on work or career with a limited link to Ravi
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about technology and work
markerNotes: Reach an overall judgement about the degree of impact, such as strong on career pathways but mostly negative on work/life balance, and support it with scenario evidence.
Weigh the benefits and costs for each area, rather than listing effects of technology on each area separately.
Treat career pathways as opportunities that the technology creates or limits, not as the training alone.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the technology without assessing how far it impacts on work/life balance or career pathways.
Stating a judgement that no example from the scenario supports.
Discussing lifestyle in general instead of Ravi's work/life balance.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Technology impacts on Ravi's work/life balance, and the effect is mostly negative. Because the company uses a cloud-based messaging app, Ravi receives work messages at night and on weekends. This extends his working day into time he would otherwise spend with family and resting, and makes it hard for him to switch off. The app also gives him some flexibility to start later after finishing work from home, so the impact is not entirely negative.
Technology has a strong positive impact on Ravi's career pathways. The company's offer of training in data analysis could open a path from technician into a new role, a move that would not be available without the technology. However, the pathway depends on his continued training and on keeping up with changing tools.
Overall, the degree of impact is significant but uneven. Technology has a considerable effect on his career pathways and a mostly negative effect on his work/life balance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides a thorough assessment with a clear judgement about the degree of impact in each area, supported by scenario evidence. Both benefits and costs are weighed, so the answer reaches the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technology impacts on Ravi's work/life balance because he gets work messages at night and on weekends, so he is not fully free from work. Technology also helps his career pathways because the company has offered him training in data analysis, which could lead to a new role. Overall, the impact on career pathways is more positive than the impact on work/life balance, although both are noticeable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides an assessment of both areas with some judgement, but the reasons for the degree of impact are brief. Explaining how the training might be limited would strengthen the judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technology means Ravi gets messages at night, which affects his work/life balance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one effect of technology on Ravi's work with a limited link to the scenario. Adding the career effect and a judgement would lift the answer.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate the rights and responsibilities of employers and employees in adopting technology in the workplace

prompts.question: Explain the rights and responsibilities of employees when adopting technology in the workplace. Provide examples to support your answer.
markerNotes: Explain rights and responsibilities separately, and give each one a workplace example, such as a new system that comes with training.
Responsibilities are actions the employee takes, such as using the technology safely and following protocols; a statement of duty without an action does not explain.
Keep to the employee's rights and responsibilities, not the employer's, which is the focus of the question.
commonStudentErrors: Giving employee rights without any responsibilities, or the reverse.
Describing the employer's rights and responsibilities instead of the employee's.
Naming a right, such as training, without an example of how it applies when new technology is adopted.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of the rights and responsibilities of employees when adopting technology in the workplace; Provides relevant examples
6 marks: Provides a sound explanation of the rights and responsibilities of employees when adopting technology in the workplace; Provides some relevant examples
4-5 marks: Provides some explanation of the rights and responsibilities of employees when adopting technology in the workplace; Provides example(s)
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of the rights and/or responsibilities of employees when using technology
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Employees have the right to be informed about how technology will impact their roles and to receive adequate training to implement the technology. Employees have the responsibility to adapt to new changes and to use the technology effectively.
For example, if a company wishes to implement a new computer operating system, the employee has the right to be adequately informed of its implementation date, so that they can be trained and prepared beforehand. Employees also have the responsibility to accept the new technology, implement it to the best of their ability, and to follow safety protocols to prevent breaches.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains the rights (to be informed and trained) and the responsibilities (to adapt, accept and use technology safely), with a workplace example of a new operating system. The example makes the explanation thorough.

sampleAnswers.answer: Employees have the right to training when a workplace introduces new technology. For example, a new software system should come with training. They also have a responsibility to use it properly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-5 row: some explanation of one right and one responsibility, with an example. Developing a second right, such as fair treatment, and linking the responsibility to safety would lift it to the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Employees have rights at work, such as training when technology is brought in.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some understanding of an employee right in relation to technology, but no responsibility and no explanation. Adding an employee responsibility and an example would move it to the 4-5 row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the security of information and copyright are issues for a small online business.

prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how security of information and copyright create issues for Lakshmi's business, explaining cause and effect for both with sound justification
5 marks: Analyses how security of information and copyright create issues for the business, with clear links to the website and videos
4 marks: Analyses one issue in some depth, or describes both issues with clear links to the business
3 marks: Describes an issue related to security of information or copyright, with a link to the business

sampleAnswers.answer:
Information and communication technology creates issues for Lakshmi's online business, and security of information is the most serious, because her website stores customers' names, addresses and card details. If the website is hacked or a login is compromised, this information could be stolen and misused, which could damage customer trust and expose the business to legal and financial consequences. The business would need secure storage and encryption, as well as regular review of who can access the data. The issue is serious because it affects both her reputation and her customers' wellbeing.
Copyright is also an issue, because the photographs and music she found online are usually owned by someone else. Using them without permission could breach copyright, and the owner could demand that the videos be removed or seek payment. Lakshmi could address this by creating her own images, buying licensed music or using material with a clear licence that permits commercial use. Both issues require careful planning as the business operates online.

sampleAnswers.answer: Security of information is an issue because the website stores customers' card details, so a hack could expose them. Copyright is also an issue because the music and photographs Lakshmi uses may belong to someone else.

dotPoints.description: Debate the issues related to the development of information and communication technologies

prompts.question: Discuss issues related to the development of information and communication technologies.
markerNotes: Discuss means weigh the issues: for each one, say what it means for individuals and whether the development of the technology makes it better or worse.
Link each issue to wellbeing (emotional, economic or physical) and use a specific example, such as a phishing email or false health claims online.
A logical structure, with one issue per paragraph and a judgement at the end about which issues matter most, earns the cohesive answer row.
commonStudentErrors: Listing issues such as privacy or copyright without discussing how each affects wellbeing.
Describing the benefits of technology when the question asks about its issues.
Using one example for all the issues instead of a specific example for each.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding about issues related to the development of information and communication technologies; Provides a clear and valid discussion about how the issues relate to the development of information and communication technologies; Provide clear links to the effect on wellbeing of individuals; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive answer
10-12 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding about issues related to the development of information and communication technologies; Provides some discussion about how the issues relate to the development of information and communication technologies; Provides a link(s) to the effect on wellbeing of individuals; Communicates information using relevant examples; Presents a cohesive answer
7-9 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of issues related to the development of information and communication technologies; Provides a link to the issues and the development of information and communication technologies; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Provides basic information about the issues and/or information and communication technologies; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about information and communication technologies and/or development of technology

sampleAnswers.answer:
The development of information and communication technologies has made life faster and more connected, but each advance also creates issues that affect the wellbeing of individuals, families and communities. The main issues are privacy and safety, security of information, accuracy of information, information overload and copyright. Each one changes how people feel, how they spend money and how safe they are.

Privacy and safety are central because connected devices and online services collect large amounts of personal data. Home security cameras and location tracking can make people feel safe, which supports emotional wellbeing, but the same tools can breach privacy when they are used without consent. The Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) regulates how many organisations handle personal information, yet many people do not read the terms they agree to, so protection depends on users as well as on the law.

Security of information is closely related. Internet banking and online shopping are convenient, but phishing emails, identity theft and credit card fraud cause financial loss and stress. A person who reuses passwords, or who logs into a bank from a public computer without logging out, is more exposed. The effect is economic and emotional, because someone who loses money to a scam may lose confidence in online services altogether.

Accuracy of information is a problem because anyone can publish online. False claims about health, such as fad diets, can lead people into unsafe practices that harm their physical wellbeing, and students who rely on unchecked websites can make poor decisions. Information overload affects wellbeing in another way. People receive many marketing emails, texts and social media posts, and algorithms track browsing, which makes it harder to identify what matters and can increase anxiety.

Copyright is the final issue. Digital copies make it easy to duplicate music, images and writing, and creators may not receive acknowledgement or payment for their work. The Copyright Act 1968 (Cth) protects creators, but enforcement is difficult across borders, which affects the economic wellbeing of artists and writers.

On balance, these issues matter most when they fall on people with less experience or fewer resources, who are the most exposed to scams, misinformation and data misuse. The development of information technology improves life for many people, but without digital literacy and stronger protections it can widen existing inequities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: discusses five issues in turn, each linked to wellbeing and a specific example, and weighs the benefits against the risks in a logical structure. The judgement at the end follows from the discussion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Information and communication technologies raise issues such as privacy and security. Online banking can be hacked and personal details can be stolen, which affects people's money and peace of mind. Many apps also collect personal data, and people may not know who is using it or how long it is kept. It is also hard to know which websites are accurate, so people may believe false information, such as health advice that is not based on evidence. Information overload is another issue, as people receive so much content on their phones that they struggle to focus or to judge what matters. Copyright is an issue too, since content can be shared without the creator being paid. Each of these issues can affect a family differently, depending on how much its members rely on online services. These issues affect wellbeing, and people need to be careful when they use new technology, especially when they are young or do not know how to protect their information.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of ICT issues such as 'Information overload', false websites and privacy, with examples, but the issues are listed rather than weighed against the benefits and the link to wellbeing is general. Discussing one issue in depth, its effect on wellbeing, and how it weighs against the benefits would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Information technology can be hacked, and people can lose their money. Some websites are not true.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: relevant information about hacking and false websites, with no discussion. Linking one issue to a person’s wellbeing would lift it to the 4-6 row.

dotPoints.description: Impact of emerging technologies (ethics; equity and access; health and safety; economic; environmental; education and learning)

prompts.question: Evaluate the impact of emerging technologies within the contexts of transport and medicine.
markerNotes: Evaluate against stated criteria, such as safety, access or ethics, and reach a verdict; a list of benefits and risks does not evaluate.
Give both transport and medicine an example developed in depth, and show the effect on the wellbeing of individuals in each.
Explain what determines the impact, such as regulation or cost, since this is what separates a judgement from a description.
commonStudentErrors: Listing benefits and risks of technology in general without applying them to transport and medicine.
Giving a verdict without criteria, such as calling a technology good or bad overall.
Describing the technology without linking its impact to the wellbeing of individuals.
Writing about technology in the home or the workplace rather than transport and medicine.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding about the impact of emerging technologies within the context of transport and medicine; Provides a well-informed judgement on the impact of emerging technologies; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of individuals; Presents a logical and cohesive response using relevant examples
10-12 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding about the impact of emerging technologies within the context of transport and medicine; Provides a judgement on the impact of emerging technologies; Provides links to the effect on the wellbeing of individuals; Communicates information using examples; Presents a cohesive response
7-9 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge about emerging technologies within the context of transport and medicine; Provides a link(s) between impact and emerging technologies; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Provides some information about emerging technologies and/or transport and/or medicine; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Emerging technologies in transport and medicine improve the wellbeing of many individuals, but the benefits are uneven and several ethical questions remain unresolved. Judged against the criteria of safety, equity and access, and ethics, the impact is strongest where a technology reduces risk or cost for many people at once, and weakest where it creates new risks that the law has not yet addressed.

In transport, autonomous vehicles are the clearest example. Their advanced sensors aim to reduce road accidents, which directly improves physical wellbeing by making travel safer for passengers, pedestrians and other drivers. They may also widen access for people who cannot drive, such as some people with disability and some older people, which supports independence and participation in community life. The ethical problems are serious, however. A vehicle may face a situation in which every option causes harm, and there is no agreed standard for how it should choose. The cost of the technology may also mean that its benefits go mainly to people who can afford new vehicles. Lighter and more fuel-efficient aircraft engines show a similar pattern: they reduce airline costs and can make cheaper flights available, which helps people on lower incomes travel, but greater access does not necessarily improve the wellbeing of every traveller.

In medicine, telehealth and new diagnostic tools expand access to care. Telehealth lets people in rural and remote areas consult a doctor without a long journey, which reduces the time, cost and fatigue of travel. The vaccines developed during the COVID-19 pandemic reduced severe illness and allowed people to return to their daily lives. Where they were free and easy to reach at pharmacies and general practices, they show how a technology can be shared fairly. Reproductive technologies such as IVF have given many people the chance of parenthood, but they raise difficult ethical questions. The fertility industry has been criticised for lacking consistent national regulation, which has allowed a single donor to father many donor-conceived children. This affects the wellbeing of those children and their families, and shows that the benefits depend on the regulation that accompanies a technology.

Overall, emerging technologies in transport and medicine have a positive impact on the wellbeing of individuals, particularly where they make travel and care safer and more accessible. Their impact is less clear where ethical and equity questions remain open, such as the decisions an autonomous vehicle makes in a crash and the regulation of donor conception. The judgement is therefore favourable but conditional: the technology improves wellbeing when governments and industry manage its risks and share its benefits fairly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 row: extensive knowledge of autonomous vehicles and medical technologies, a well-informed judgement against stated criteria, and clear links to the wellbeing of individuals in both contexts. The verdict is conditional and argued, which is what separates an evaluation from a list.

sampleAnswers.answer: Emerging technologies in transport and medicine have a mostly positive impact on individuals. Autonomous vehicles use sensors to reduce road accidents, which improves physical safety, and they may help people who cannot drive. Aircraft engines that burn less fuel can make cheaper flights available. However, autonomous vehicles raise ethical issues about how they should act in a crash, and the technology may be expensive, so not everyone benefits. In medicine, telehealth allows people in remote areas to see a doctor without travelling, which improves access to care. Reproductive technologies such as IVF bring benefits to families but also ethical concerns, because the fertility industry has been criticised for lacking consistent national regulation. Overall, these technologies improve wellbeing for many people, but the benefits are not shared equally and the ethical questions are not fully answered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of autonomous vehicles, telehealth and reproductive technologies, with an example for each and a link to wellbeing. The overall judgement is stated but not argued against criteria, and the equity point is brief. Testing the benefits against equity and ethics in more depth would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Driverless cars and telehealth are new technologies. They help people travel and see doctors, but some people may not be able to use them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: some relevant information about two technologies, with no evaluation and little link to wellbeing. Naming a benefit and a risk for each context, and saying who is affected, would lift it to the 4-6 row.

prompts.scenario:
Your answer will be assessed on how well you:

prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Examine various emerging technologies and predict the potential impact of their development

prompts.question: Predict TWO potential impacts on the community if a council trials driverless buses on its main routes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is considering a trial of driverless buses on its main bus routes. Driverless buses are an emerging technology, and council staff want to understand how they could affect residents, bus drivers and other road users before deciding.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Predicts two potential impacts of driverless buses on the community, with reasons based on the trial
2 marks: Predicts one potential impact of driverless buses on the community, with a limited reason
1 mark: Identifies a possible effect of driverless buses on residents or drivers
markerNotes: State each predicted impact as something that could happen, then give the reason, such as fewer crashes caused by human error.
Use both a benefit and a cost, or two different groups, so the prediction is not one-sided.
Predictions should be hedged, such as could or may, and tied to the trial rather than stated as certain.
commonStudentErrors: Stating an impact as certain, such as 'driverless buses will remove all crashes'.
Predicting two impacts that are really the same point, such as two kinds of job loss.
Describing what driverless buses are rather than predicting an impact on the community.

sampleAnswers.answer: The potential impact of driverless buses on the community is predicted to be mixed. As an emerging technology, they could improve road safety, because many crashes involve human error and automated systems do not become tired or distracted. However, bus drivers may lose their jobs, which could create financial hardship for some families and reduce local employment. Residents with limited mobility might benefit from more frequent services, although this depends on how the council plans the routes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts two potential impacts, one benefit and one cost, each with a reason. The answer uses hedged language that fits a prediction about a trial.

sampleAnswers.answer: Driverless buses could make roads safer, but bus drivers may lose their jobs as the technology is introduced.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts one potential impact with a reason and gives a second impact briefly. Making the second prediction fully developed would earn the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Driverless buses could change how people travel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a possible effect of the technology, but does not predict an impact on the community.

prompts.question: Examine the two emerging technologies described and their potential impact on patients and health care staff.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional health service is planning its next five years of investment. It is considering two emerging technologies: telehealth consultations, which allow patients to see clinicians by video, and wearable devices that monitor heart rate and sleep. The service wants a clear picture of the benefits and drawbacks for patients and staff.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a thorough examination of both emerging technologies and their potential impact on patients and health care staff, with well-supported reasoning
5 marks: Provides a sound examination of both emerging technologies, with clear links to their potential impact on patients or staff
4 marks: Examines both technologies, with some links to their potential impact
3 marks: Describes one emerging technology and its potential impact on patients or staff
2 marks: Identifies an emerging technology with a limited link to its potential impact
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about emerging technologies in health care
markerNotes: Examine each technology separately, with benefits and drawbacks for patients and for staff, then compare the two briefly.
Use the scenario details, such as remote access or continuous monitoring, to explain each impact.
A list of advantages with no reasoning about who is affected stays in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Examining only one of the two technologies in depth.
Describing what telehealth or wearable devices are without explaining their potential impact.
Discussing patients only, when the question also asks about health care staff.

sampleAnswers.answer:
These two emerging technologies have different effects. Telehealth allows patients to consult doctors, nurses or specialists by video or phone, which can improve access for people in rural areas or those with limited mobility. For patients, the potential impact is reduced travel and time off work. However, not all patients have reliable internet or the digital skills to use it, so the benefits may be unevenly shared. For health care staff, telehealth can reduce pressure on clinic rooms, but it may increase workloads if consultations are poorly scheduled.
Wearable devices that monitor heart rate and sleep can give patients and clinicians continuous information, allowing problems to be detected early and encouraging healthier habits. Their potential impact on patients includes greater self-management of conditions. However, the data they collect raises privacy concerns, and staff may face more alerts to review. Overall, both technologies have strong potential to improve care, but their impact depends on access, privacy and how well staff are supported.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines both technologies, with benefits and drawbacks for patients and staff explained through the scenario. The overall judgement is supported and reaches the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Telehealth lets patients in remote areas consult a doctor by video, which can reduce travel. Wearable devices can monitor heart rate, but staff may need to review more data. Both technologies have a potential impact on patients and health care staff, although the effects differ between the two.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Examines both technologies with some links to their impact, but the effects on patients and staff are not developed. Explaining one drawback for each technology would lift the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Telehealth lets people see a doctor online, and wearable devices track health.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies an emerging technology with a limited link to its potential impact. Explaining who is affected and how would strengthen it.

dotPoints.description: Issues related to technological development (reasons for the development of the technology; factors affecting access to and acceptance of the technology; impact on lifestyle and wellbeing of the technology)

prompts.question: Analyse how an individual’s access to and acceptance of a selected piece of technology can affect their lifestyle.
markerNotes: Analyse access and acceptance separately and then together, since a person may have access but not accept the technology, and each combination shapes lifestyle differently.
Link each effect to the individual's wellbeing, such as emotional wellbeing from family contact or financial wellbeing from avoided costs.
Use one or two concrete examples from the selected technology rather than listing many.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the benefits of the technology without addressing access or acceptance.
Treating access and acceptance as the same thing.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Provides an extensive analysis of how an individual’s access to and acceptance of a selected piece of technology affects their lifestyle; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of the individual; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive response
10-12 marks: Provides a thorough analysis of how an individual’s access to and acceptance of a selected piece of technology affects their lifestyle; Provides link(s) to the effect on the wellbeing of the individual; Communicates information using examples; Presents a cohesive response
7-9 marks: Provides an analysis of how an individual’s access to and/or acceptance of a selected piece of technology affects their lifestyle; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of an individual’s access to and/or acceptance of a select piece of technology and/or how it affects their lifestyle; Provide example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about individual’s access to and/or acceptance of technology

sampleAnswers.answer:
The mobile phone shows how access to and acceptance of a technology can shape an individual's lifestyle. Access depends on cost, skills and where a person lives, while acceptance depends on age, culture and confidence. When both are present, the phone can improve wellbeing, but when either is missing, the individual may be left out of ordinary daily life.

Access comes first. A person with a smartphone and a data plan can bank, book appointments and keep in touch with family from home. A household on a low income may see a phone as a low priority beside food, clothing and shelter, so its members lose these conveniences and spend more time and money on tasks that could be done online. The COVID-19 lockdowns exposed this gap, as families with limited internet access or few devices struggled to keep children on task with remote learning and fell further behind their peers.

Acceptance matters just as much. A person may own a phone but not use it confidently because of age, culture or a lack of skill, and this narrows their lifestyle. An older person who does not accept the phone may miss family contact or be unable to use online services, so they must travel or rely on others for tasks they could manage alone. Cultural norms about privacy or about how families communicate can also shape how readily a person adopts the device.

The effect on wellbeing follows from these two factors together. Connection with others supports emotional wellbeing, and access to services supports physical and financial wellbeing. Because phones are now used for banking, health bookings and government services, a person who lacks access or acceptance may face extra costs or delays, which increases stress and reduces independence. A person who has both access and acceptance may gain time for family, work and study, which improves the balance of daily life.

Technology also creates new pressures. Constant availability can make it hard to switch off, and a person who readily accepts the phone may spend more time on screens and less on face-to-face relationships. Acceptance therefore has both positive and negative effects, and the lifestyle outcome depends on how the individual uses the device rather than on owning it.

Overall, access and acceptance shape lifestyle to a considerable extent. Access determines whether the phone is available to a person at all, and acceptance determines whether it becomes part of daily routines. The strongest positive effects occur when both are present and supported by the person's wider network, while the greatest disadvantage comes from being excluded from both.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: it analyses how access and acceptance of a mobile phone each change lifestyle, links each to the individual's wellbeing, and uses examples such as remote learning. A firmer view on which factor matters more for a given person would lift it further.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Access and acceptance both affect how a person lives when they use a mobile phone. A person who has a phone but cannot afford data may find it hard to bank or book appointments online, which limits their lifestyle. Some older people may own a phone but not use it, and this can mean they miss contact with family.

The COVID-19 lockdowns showed how access matters. Many families without enough devices found it hard to keep children learning at home, which affected their wellbeing. Access also depends on where a person lives, because a weak signal can limit what the phone can do.

Acceptance can change lifestyle too. A person who does not feel confident with the phone may avoid using it for tasks such as banking, which takes time away from other activities. A person who accepts the phone may find it helps them keep in touch with others, but constant use can also affect relationships. Overall, access and acceptance both shape lifestyle, though the effects depend on the individual.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: it analyses access and acceptance with examples, but the wellbeing links are brief and the examples are less developed than in a top answer. Developing the wellbeing link for each factor would move it into the 10–12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A mobile phone lets people call and text each other. Some people have phones and others do not. Phones can also be used for banking and for keeping in touch with family.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: it gives relevant information about the phone but does not analyse access or acceptance or their effect on lifestyle. Choosing one factor and explaining its effect on the individual would move it up.
