prompts.question: Analyse how workplace structures can influence the efficiency of employees in a workplace.
markerNotes: Analyse the mechanism: each structure affects efficiency by changing how supported, safe or distracted employees are, so explain that effect rather than listing structures.
Link each structure to the wellbeing of the employee and the employer, such as lower stress or fewer days lost to injury.
Develop two or three concrete structures fully, such as flexible arrangements or on-site childcare.
commonStudentErrors: Listing workplace structures, such as a staff kitchen or a prayer room, without explaining how they change efficiency.
Assuming every structure always improves efficiency without considering when it does not.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Provides an extensive analysis of how workplace structures can influence the efficiency of the workplace; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of employees; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive response
10-12 marks: Provides a thorough analysis of how workplace structures can influence the efficiency of the workplace; Provides link(s) to the effect on the wellbeing of employees; Communicates information using relevant examples; Presents a cohesive response
7-9 marks: Provides an analysis of how workplace structure(s) can influence the efficiency of the workplace; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of workplace structure(s) that influence the efficiency of the workplace; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about workplace structure(s) and/or efficiency of the workplace

sampleAnswers.answer:
Workplace structures influence efficiency because they shape how supported, safe and valued employees feel, and this affects both how much they produce and how well they cope with their work. Some structures are required by law, while others depend on the employer's choices. Together they affect the wellbeing of employees as well as the productivity of the business.

Workplace culture initiatives are one example. A prayer room lets staff meet their religious obligations on site, so they do not need to leave and lose time. A staff kitchen lets workers eat and gather socially close to their work, which helps them feel supported and cuts the time spent buying lunch or travelling. Both reduce time lost and can improve morale, which supports efficiency.

On-site childcare is another structure. Employees who know their children are cared for nearby can work more productively, and they avoid the lost time of leaving early to collect a child. The link to wellbeing is clear, because parents who are less anxious about childcare can focus on their tasks, which lowers stress and supports their emotional wellbeing.

Flexible work arrangements also matter. Under the National Employment Standards in the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), eligible employees can request flexible working arrangements, and many employers negotiate staggered start and finish times. A worker who can drop off and collect children is less distracted by those commitments during the working day. The employer keeps a skilled worker, and the employee's work-family balance improves, which contributes to efficiency.

Legal structures shape efficiency too. Work health and safety laws, such as the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW), require employers to manage risks, so employees can work without fear of injury. When employees feel safe they are more likely to concentrate on their tasks, and the workplace avoids the costs of injury and lost time.

Structures can also reduce efficiency when they are poorly designed. A rigid rule about start times may frustrate employees with caring duties, and a grievance procedure that is slow or unfair may leave staff disengaged. Structures therefore improve efficiency only when employees trust that they will be applied fairly.

Overall, workplace structures influence efficiency most strongly when they support employees' wellbeing as well as meeting legal duties. Where childcare, flexible arrangements and safety systems are in place, staff are more likely to work productively and to stay, and the employer gains from that. Where these structures are missing or poorly designed, the same arrangements become a source of stress and lost time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13–15 row: it analyses how culture initiatives, childcare, flexible arrangements and safety law each affect efficiency, links them to employee wellbeing, and uses examples throughout. A clearer judgement on when structures fail to improve efficiency would strengthen the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Workplace structures can affect efficiency by making employees feel supported. A staff kitchen or a prayer room means workers do not need to leave the site, which saves time and lets them focus on their work.

Flexible work arrangements also matter. A worker who can negotiate staggered start and finish times can drop off and collect children from childcare, so they are less distracted during the day. This supports their wellbeing and their productivity.

Health and safety laws are another structure. Employers must manage risks under work health and safety legislation, and employees who feel safe are more likely to work without fear of injury. This means fewer days lost and a more efficient workplace.

Overall, these structures improve efficiency, although a poorly designed rule can frustrate employees and reduce how well they work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7–9 row: it analyses how supportive structures and flexible arrangements affect efficiency, with examples, but the links to wellbeing are brief and the examples are less developed than in a top answer. Developing the wellbeing link for each structure would move it into the 10–12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A workplace may have a prayer room, a staff kitchen and childcare. Employers must follow work health and safety laws. Workers are entitled to some leave.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1–3 row: it names workplace structures and a legal duty, but does not analyse how they affect efficiency. Explaining one structure's effect on how employees work would move it up.

prompts.scenario:
Your answer will be assessed on how well you:
• demonstrate knowledge and understanding of societal influences on wellbeing relevant to the question
• apply the skills of critical thinking and analysis
• communicate ideas and information using relevant examples
• present a logical and cohesive response
prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

prompts.question: Describe how workplace culture can contribute to efficient work practices.
markerNotes: Describe the mechanism: a workplace feature such as a prayer room or childcare cuts time away from work or raises motivation, which then makes work more efficient.
Give a specific workplace example for each feature described, which earns the example mark at the 3-mark level.
Define efficient work practices in terms of productivity, retention or morale, not just as working hard.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a friendly team culture without linking it to efficiency.
Writing about workplace rights or safety rules rather than workplace culture.
Defining efficiency as working faster, without describing how the culture helps the work.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Provides a thorough description about how workplace culture contributes to efficient work practices; Provides relevant examples
3 marks: Provides a sound description about how workplace culture contributes to efficient work practices; Provides an example(s)
2 marks: Provides some information about workplace culture and/or efficient work practices
1 mark: Provides relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Workplace culture includes facilities such as a prayer room, kitchen and childcare. Efficient work practices refers to high productivity with minimal effort and can include high staff retention, greater work satisfaction and improved staff morale. A positive workplace culture enhances efficiency in the workplace and promotes productivity and decreases absenteeism.
The provision of a prayer room supports an individual’s religious commitments and therefore results in the employee working more efficiently due to less time away from the workplace and more time to commit to tasks. They may also feel more supported in the workplace and experience work satisfaction, therefore being more motivated to perform. Similarly, a kitchen in the workplace provides opportunities for social interaction and collaboration alongside a place to make healthy meals, increasing workplace satisfaction.
The provision of childcare allows for an employee to decrease their travel time to an alternative childcare provider and can be an incentive for a parent to return to the workplace, therefore retaining qualified staff.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: describes how a prayer room, a kitchen and childcare each make work more efficient, through less time away, more motivation and retention, with examples.

sampleAnswers.answer: A workplace culture that is friendly and supportive makes people want to come to work and stay in their jobs. When staff feel valued, they are less likely to leave, and this can help them work better because they do not have to keep learning new tasks. Staff who feel comfortable with colleagues also tend to ask questions sooner, which helps the work get done.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: some information about a friendly workplace and efficiency, 'makes people want to come to work', with no named feature and no example. Naming one feature, such as childcare, and how it saves time would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Workplace culture is the way people behave at work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: a relevant definition of culture, with no link to efficiency. Describing one way culture improves work would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Examine the extent to which the workplace can provide equal access to work entitlements for females and males

prompts.question: Explain how access to leave entitlements can help provide equality for males and females in the workplace.
markerNotes: Explain how the entitlement gives both men and women equal access, such as parental leave for either parent, and what the result is for the workplace or family.
Name the leave entitlement and who can access it, then show the effect on equity, such as fathers taking leave as well as mothers.
Test the equality claim: an entitlement can be equally available on paper while unspoken pressures or industry patterns limit who uses it.
commonStudentErrors: Describing leave entitlements without explaining how they give males and females equal access.
Stating that men and women both have leave, without explaining how it promotes equality in the workplace.
Assuming leave entitlements alone create equality, without considering whether everyone uses them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of how access to leave entitlements can help provide equal access for both males and females in the workplace
5 marks: Provides a sound explanation of how access to leave entitlements can help provide equal access for both males and females in the workplace
4 marks: Provides an explanation of how leave entitlements can help provide equal access for both males and females in the workplace
2-3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of workplace structures and/or equal access for males and/or females in the workplace
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Both males and females have equal access to leave entitlements. Following a birth or adoption, both males and females are entitled to access both paid and unpaid parental leave to care for a child. By giving parents approved time off and the right to return to work, employers are able to retain skilled and experienced workers. Even though both male and females have equal access to parental leave, there may be unspoken pressure on males in the workplace to return to work early.
Carers leave is an award condition that is available to both men and women to allow them to care for family members when they are ill and still receive an income. Even though both females and males have access, it tends to be women that access carers leave more than men due to the industry that they are employed or due to their nurturing nature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: explains how parental leave and carers leave give males and females equal access and links this to retaining workers, then tests the claim by noting unspoken pressure and differences in use. The answer does not stop at the entitlement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Leave entitlements let parents take time off to care for a child, so both mothers and fathers can look after their children. Both parents can take this time off to care for the child, and the leave is set out in legislation and workplace awards, so it applies across most jobs and does not depend on the parent's gender.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 row: some understanding of how leave gives both sexes access, 'so both mothers and fathers can look after their children', with the entitlement named. The answer does not explain how this promotes equality in the workplace, and adding that would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Men and women both get some leave at work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: some relevant information about leave, with no explanation of equal access. Explaining what the leave allows each parent to do would lift it to the 2-3 mark row.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Individual roles (personal commitments and interests (work; leadership; parenting; caring; volunteering; religion; recreation; studying; hobbies))

prompts.question: Describe two of Mei's personal commitments or interests and the individual role each one gives her.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Mei is 19 and studies nursing part-time at university. She works 12 hours a week at a cafe, volunteers at an animal shelter on Saturdays, plays netball on Thursday nights and cares for her grandmother, who lives with the family and needs help with daily tasks.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two personal commitments or interests and explains the individual role each one gives Mei, with clear links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes two personal commitments or interests and links each one to a role Mei holds
2 marks: Identifies personal commitments or interests with a limited link to Mei's individual roles
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about personal commitments or interests
markerNotes: Name two commitments or interests from Mei's situation, then state the individual role that each one gives her.
Credit roles such as student, carer, volunteer or team member, provided the link to the commitment is clear.
A list of commitments with no role attached stays in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Listing commitments without explaining the role each one gives Mei.
Overlooking the caring role because it is unpaid and not part of a formal job.
Describing the commitments in general terms without reference to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two of Mei's personal commitments are studying and caring. Her part-time nursing degree gives her one of her individual roles, as a student, and it shapes her time, her goals and the way she plans her week. Caring for her grandmother adds another of her individual roles, as carer at home, as she helps with daily tasks that other family members might otherwise share. Her volunteering at an animal shelter is a personal interest that gives her a role as a volunteer, connecting her with the community and giving her a break from study and family responsibilities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two commitments and explains the individual role each gives Mei, with clear links to the scenario. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mei has a part-time job at a cafe and volunteers at an animal shelter. The job gives her the role of employee. Volunteering gives her a role in the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two commitments but gives only a brief role for each, with little explanation of how they shape Mei's life. This sits in the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mei studies nursing and looks after her grandmother.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names the commitments without describing the role either one gives Mei. This is the bottom row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the mix of personal commitments and interests in Tomas's life shapes the individual roles he can sustain across work, family and community.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Tomas is 45, a father of three and an electrician. He coaches his son's under-12 soccer team, sings in his local church choir and has recently taken on a second job on weekends to pay for a home renovation. He now has little time for his hobbies.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses in detail how the mix of personal commitments and interests shapes the individual roles Tomas can sustain, with precise links across his work, family and community life
5 marks: Analyses how the mix of personal commitments and interests shapes Tomas's individual roles, with clear links to his wellbeing
4 marks: Explains how Tomas's personal commitments and interests affect the roles he holds, with relevant links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes some personal commitments or interests and links them to Tomas's roles
2 marks: Identifies a personal commitment or interest with a limited link to Tomas's roles
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about personal commitments or interests
markerNotes: Judge how far the commitments can be sustained together, then explain the effect on Tomas's roles and wellbeing.
Use the scenario details, such as the weekend second job and the coaching, to show the competing demands on his time.
Credit an answer that weighs a commitment that builds one role, such as coaching as leadership and parenting, against the time it takes from another.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each commitment separately without analysing how they compete for time.
Writing about work-life balance in general rather than Tomas's individual roles.
Treating coaching as only a hobby without linking it to leadership or parenting.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tomas's personal commitments and interests show how a mix of roles can compete for limited time. His work as an electrician and his second weekend job take up most of his week, which reduces the time he has for parenting his three children. Coaching his son's soccer team is a form of leadership that strengthens his parenting role and his connection to the community, but it also uses weekend time that could go to rest. His choir membership gives him a sense of belonging, yet the renovation pressures mean he has little time for his hobbies. Because these commitments overlap, Tomas can sustain his individual roles only if he prioritises the commitments that matter most to his family and his wellbeing. Without that choice, the time pressure could spill over into his parenting, his health and the quality of his coaching, so each commitment needs regular review.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses how the commitments compete and how each one shapes a role, with precise links to the scenario. The judgement at the end is well supported, so this meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tomas has many commitments, including work, parenting, coaching and choir. Taking on a second job means he has less time for his family and his hobbies. Coaching gives him a leadership role, but it takes up weekend time. These commitments affect the individual roles he holds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how the commitments affect Tomas's roles with relevant links to the scenario, but the competing demands are listed rather than analysed. This sits in the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tomas coaches his son's soccer team and works as an electrician. He also has a second job and sings in a choir.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies several commitments with a limited link to his roles and no analysis. This is the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Recognise that individuals may have multiple roles outside the workplace

prompts.question: Outline three roles that Sam holds outside the workplace, and state one responsibility that comes with each role.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Sam is 34 and works as a shift supervisor at a distribution centre. Outside work, he is a parent of two primary school children, coaches a junior football team on Saturday mornings and is the volunteer treasurer for his local Scouts group.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines three roles Sam holds outside the workplace and states a specific responsibility for each one
3 marks: Outlines three roles Sam holds outside the workplace, with a responsibility stated for most of them
2 marks: Identifies two roles Sam holds outside the workplace with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about roles outside the workplace
markerNotes: Name three roles first, then give the responsibility that goes with each one, using the scenario.
Credit roles such as parent, coach and volunteer, as long as each is clearly outside the workplace.
A list of roles with no responsibility stated stays in the middle rows.
commonStudentErrors: Naming Sam's shift supervisor role, which is inside the workplace.
Listing roles without stating any responsibility for them.
Giving the responsibilities without naming the role they belong to.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sam has multiple roles outside the workplace. First, he is a parent of two primary school children, and his responsibility is to provide care, school support and transport for them. Second, he coaches a junior football team on Saturday mornings, where his responsibility is to plan training sessions and keep players safe. Third, he is a volunteer treasurer for the local Scouts group, and his responsibility is to keep accurate financial records and report to members. Each of these roles exists alongside his work as a shift supervisor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines three roles outside the workplace, each with a specific responsibility drawn from the scenario. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sam is a parent and a football coach. He coaches on Saturday mornings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two roles outside the workplace with limited detail and no responsibilities stated. This is the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sam is a parent of two children.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides one relevant role without any detail. This is the bottom row.

prompts.question: Discuss how recognising that individuals hold multiple roles outside the workplace could shape the way an employer supports an employee like Leila.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Leila is 29 and works as an accounts officer for a regional council. She studies a part-time Master of Business at night, has a partner who works rotating shifts, and volunteers as a reader at her son's primary school.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses in detail how recognising multiple roles outside the workplace could shape employer support, with a balanced consideration of its benefits and limits for Leila
5 marks: Discusses how recognising multiple roles outside the workplace could shape employer support for Leila, with clear links to her wellbeing
4 marks: Explains how an employer could support an employee with multiple roles outside the workplace, with relevant links to Leila
3 marks: Describes some ways an employer could support an employee with multiple roles
2 marks: Identifies a role outside the workplace with a limited link to employer support
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about multiple roles
markerNotes: Discuss both sides: how recognising the roles helps the employer and the employee, and where the support has limits.
Use Leila's specific roles, such as study nights and rotating shifts, to show what the employer could change.
Credit a response that links flexible arrangements to wellbeing and productivity rather than only listing them.
commonStudentErrors: Describing flexible work without linking it to recognising Leila's multiple roles.
Discussing only the benefits and not the limits or fairness to other staff.
Treating the employer's support as a legal entitlement without any discussion of it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Recognising that individuals hold multiple roles outside the workplace means an employer sees the whole person, not only the employee. For Leila, a part-time Master of Business, a partner on rotating shifts and her school volunteering all compete for the same hours. An employer who understands these multiple roles could offer flexible work arrangements, such as later starts on study nights or swapping shifts to match her partner's roster. This support can improve Leila's wellbeing, reduce stress and make her more productive at work. However, the benefits depend on workplace culture and on whether the arrangements are fair to other staff, so the employer must balance individual needs with the needs of the team. Clear communication, written agreements and regular review would help both Leila and her colleagues understand what is expected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the benefits and limits of recognising multiple roles for Leila and the employer, with clear links to the scenario. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An employer who knows that Leila has multiple roles outside the workplace could offer some flexibility, such as later starts on study days. This would help her manage her study and family commitments. It may also improve her wellbeing at work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains one way an employer could support Leila with relevant links, but the discussion is brief and does not weigh the limits. This is the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Leila studies at night and her partner works shifts. An employer could let her change her hours.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies roles and one form of support with limited discussion. This is the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Individual strategies for managing multiple roles (negotiating and sharing roles; managing resources; using technology; accessing support; utilising workplace structures)

prompts.question: How can individuals use technology to manage multiple role expectations?
markerNotes: Name a specific technology and the role expectation it helps with, such as online grocery shopping for household tasks, then explain what time or energy it frees.
Explain how the freed time helps the individual balance roles, such as more time for children's sport or for social obligations.
commonStudentErrors: Naming a technology without saying which role expectation it helps manage.
Writing about the employer's technology rather than the individual's own use.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of how individuals can use technology to manage multiple role expectations
3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of how individuals can use technology to manage multiple role expectations
2 marks: Demonstrates a limited understanding of how individuals can use technology to manage multiple role expectations
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: An individual could use the Internet and online shopping technology to save time with household tasks. Groceries can be ordered online and delivered to a person’s home, enabling the individual to satisfy the domestic and organisational tasks, leaving more time to take their children to organised sporting activities. Labour saving devices such as robotic vacuum cleaners and dishwashers allow busy individuals who may work long hours to spend less time with household tasks and more time with family or friends, satisfying social obligations.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the sound-understanding row: it explains how online grocery shopping and labour saving appliances free time for family and social roles. Linking this to a specific role conflict, such as work hours, would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: An individual could use online shopping to buy groceries, which saves the time of going to the shops and carrying heavy bags home, and the groceries can be delivered straight to the home.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: names online shopping and explains that it 'saves the time of going to the shops', but does not show how the technology helps manage multiple roles. Linking the saved time to a specific role, such as work or caring, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Many people use computers at home.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information only: no role expectation is addressed.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (25 marks). Attempt ONE question from Questions 30–32. Allow about 45 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Devise strategies that individuals can utilise to effectively manage multiple role expectations caused by changing circumstances

prompts.question: Describe two strategies Priya could use to manage her multiple role expectations after these changes in circumstances.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Priya is 41 and works full-time as a pharmacist. Her employer has restructured her department, which has added an extra day to her working week. Her father, who lives nearby, has had a stroke and now needs help with meals and medical appointments three days a week, and her son's sport training has moved to early mornings.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two strategies Priya could use and explains how each one helps her manage her multiple role expectations
3 marks: Describes two strategies Priya could use to manage her role expectations, with a link to her changed circumstances
2 marks: Identifies strategies for managing role expectations with a limited link to Priya
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about managing multiple roles
markerNotes: Name each strategy, then explain how it helps Priya meet her role expectations after the changes.
Credit strategies such as negotiating a roster, sharing tasks, or planning time, when linked to the scenario.
A strategy stated without explanation of how it works stays in the lower rows.
commonStudentErrors: Naming strategies that do not relate to Priya's changed circumstances.
Describing Priya's roles without describing a strategy.
Giving two versions of the same strategy, such as talking to family and sharing tasks, as separate strategies.

sampleAnswers.answer: Priya could use negotiating roles with her employer, asking for a set roster that fits her restructured week and protects time for her father's appointments. These strategies help her manage multiple role expectations because they give her some control over when she works. A second of her strategies is sharing responsibilities with her partner and son, so that transport to sport and household tasks are divided. Shared responsibilities reduce the pressure on Priya, which helps her respond to changing circumstances without becoming overloaded.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two strategies and explains how each one helps Priya manage her role expectations after the changes. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Priya could ask her employer for a set roster. She could also share tasks with her family.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two strategies with little explanation of how they help Priya. This is the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Priya could talk to her family about her hours.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides one relevant idea without describing how it manages her roles. This is the bottom row.

prompts.question: Construct a strategy plan that Daniel could use to manage his multiple role expectations as his changing circumstances affect his work, study and family.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Daniel is 27 and works as a childcare educator who has been offered a promotion that requires supervising a second centre. He is also studying a diploma in the evenings and is now the main support for his younger brother, who has moved in with him after a change in living arrangements.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a sound and detailed strategy plan specific to Daniel's work, study and family roles, with clear justification of how each strategy manages his multiple role expectations
5 marks: Constructs a sound strategy plan that manages Daniel's multiple role expectations, with clear links to his changing circumstances
4 marks: Develops relevant strategies for Daniel, with some links to his multiple role expectations
3 marks: Identifies some strategies for managing role expectations with limited links to Daniel's circumstances
2 marks: Identifies a strategy with a limited link to managing multiple roles
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about managing role expectations
markerNotes: Build the plan as a set of connected strategies, each tied to a specific role Daniel holds.
Justify why each strategy suits the changes in his work, study and family, not only what the strategy is.
Credit a plan that includes a review step, because circumstances keep changing.
commonStudentErrors: Listing generic strategies such as time management without applying them to Daniel's roles.
Constructing a plan that ignores one of the three roles, such as the brother's care.
Describing the changes in Daniel's circumstances without building any strategy from them.

sampleAnswers.answer: Daniel's first strategy is negotiating roles with his employer. He could ask for the supervisory role to start after his diploma assessments are complete, or for a phased handover, so that his workload changes gradually. Second, he should set up a time management system, using a shared calendar that blocks study nights, rostered shifts and set times for supporting his brother. This makes his multiple role expectations visible to everyone. Third, he could arrange a shared support plan with family or a community service, so his brother's needs are met on evenings he is studying. Finally, Daniel should schedule regular wellbeing check-ins, so he can review the plan as his changing circumstances evolve. Together these strategies allow him to manage multiple role expectations without giving up his promotion or his study.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a plan of connected strategies, each tied to a role and justified against the changes. The review step and the closing justification meet the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Daniel could ask his employer to phase in the new role. He could also use a shared calendar to manage multiple role expectations, blocking study nights and set times to support his brother. This helps him deal with changing circumstances.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Develops two relevant strategies with some links to his roles, but the plan is not justified or complete. This is the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Daniel could make a calendar of his study and work. This helps him see his time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one strategy with a limited link to his roles. This is the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Issues that impact on youth employment (personal management skills required in the workplace; steps taken to prepare and plan for a career; predominant patterns of work of young people; rights and responsibilities of young people in the workplace)

prompts.question: Analyse how youth employment issues can affect a young person’s employment opportunities.
markerNotes: Analyse how each issue changes a young person’s chances, such as a lack of interview practice reducing the number of offers, rather than listing the issues.
Use the specifics of the syllabus, such as VET qualifications, work experience, award rates or the Fair Work Ombudsman, and link each to the young person’s wellbeing.
Make the judgement explicit, saying which issue most limits opportunities and why, which the logical and cohesive row asks for.
commonStudentErrors: Describing youth employment in general, such as young people finding it hard to get jobs, without analysing a specific issue.
Listing the issues without linking any of them to a young person’s employment opportunities.
Writing about older workers or the whole workforce rather than young people.
prompts.markingCriteria:
13-15 marks: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding about youth employment issues; Provides a clear and valid analysis about how youth employment issues can affect a young person’s employment opportunities; Provides clear links to the effect on the wellbeing of young people; Communicates ideas and information using relevant examples; Presents a logical and cohesive answer
10-12 marks: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding about youth employment issues; Provides some analysis about how youth employment issues can affect a young person’s employment opportunities; Provides a link(s) to the effect on the wellbeing of young people; Communicates information using relevant examples; Presents a cohesive answer
7-9 marks: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding about youth employment issue(s); Provides a link to how youth employment issue(s) can affect a young person’s employment opportunities; Communicates some information using examples
4-6 marks: Provides basic information about employment opportunities and/or youth employment and/or issues that impact on youth employment; Provides example(s)
1-3 marks: Provides relevant information about employment opportunities and/or youth employment

sampleAnswers.answer:
Youth employment issues shape a young person’s opportunities by affecting which jobs they can get, how well they keep them and whether they can build a career. The main issues are the personal management skills they bring to work, the steps they take to prepare for a career, the patterns of work open to young people, and whether they know their rights and responsibilities. Each one affects both their income and their wellbeing.

Personal management skills are a major influence on whether a young person is hired and kept on. Employers look for communication, organisation, problem solving and decision making, and a young person who lacks these may struggle in an interview or in the first months of a job. A young person who has built these skills through part-time work, school leadership or volunteering is better placed, and the confidence gained improves their chances of advancement.

Preparing for a career also matters. Completing the HSC, taking part in work experience, enrolling in a vocational education and training (VET) course with a nationally recognised qualification, or attending TAFE or university all widen the range of jobs a young person can apply for. A young person with a clear resume and practice at interviews is more competitive. One who leaves school without a plan may have fewer options and may take casual work that offers little security.

The patterns of work available to young people are often casual, part-time or voluntary. These can suit study, but they offer fewer hours, less job security and fewer chances to build a long-term career. Youth unemployment is usually higher than adult unemployment, so a young person who cannot find stable work may face financial stress, which can reduce their confidence and their willingness to keep applying.

Rights and responsibilities also shape opportunities. A young person who does not know their rights may be paid below the award rate, not paid for all hours worked, or refused leave entitlements. The Fair Work Ombudsman can help them check their entitlements, and the Fair Work Commission sets minimum wages and award rates. Understanding responsibilities, such as following reasonable instructions and being punctual, helps a young person keep a job once they have it.

On balance, a young person’s opportunities depend on both their own preparation and the support they receive. A young person with good skills, a clear plan and knowledge of their rights is in a strong position, while one who lacks these may be pushed into insecure work. Over time this limits both their employment opportunities and their wellbeing, which is why the early years of work matter so much.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the top row: analyses four issues (personal skills, career preparation, patterns of work and rights) and links each to a young person’s opportunities and wellbeing, with specific examples such as VET qualifications and award rates. The answer reaches a judgement on which issue matters most.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people often lack work experience, so employers may not hire them. Many employers ask for a history of work, and a young person who has never had a job may find that their application is passed over in favour of someone with a track record. Some take casual jobs, which give little security. Casual hours can change from week to week, which makes it hard to plan study, rent or other commitments, and the lack of paid leave means that a young person who is sick may lose pay. They also need to know their rights at work, or they can be taken advantage of. A young person who does not know about minimum wages or penalty rates may be paid less than the award requires, which affects both their income and their confidence to apply for other jobs. Young people also face the cost of training, such as TAFE courses or certificates, which many cannot afford while they are working or studying. Overall, these issues can make it harder for young people to find work and keep it, and they affect their wellbeing as well as their income.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 row: sound knowledge of youth employment issues, with examples such as 'a young person who has never had a job', and a link to opportunities, but the issues are listed rather than analysed in depth. Explaining one specific issue, such as no work experience, in full and its effect on wellbeing would lift it to the 10-12 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people need jobs, and it can be hard for them to get one. Some do not have much experience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 row: relevant information about youth jobs, with no analysis of an issue. Naming one issue and how it limits employment opportunities would lift it to the 4-6 row.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a case study of the issues that impact on youth employment by considering the following questions: what are the factors contributing to youth unemployment?; how can a young person optimise their employment prospects?; how does work support young people to manage multiple roles?

prompts.question: Outline three factors contributing to youth unemployment, using Lachlan's situation to illustrate one of them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Lachlan is 18 and is completing Year 12 at a school in regional NSW. He works 12 hours a week at a supermarket, is applying for an apprenticeship in carpentry, and has few local employers he can reach by public transport.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines three factors contributing to youth unemployment and uses Lachlan's situation to illustrate one of them accurately
3 marks: Outlines three factors contributing to youth unemployment, with a link to Lachlan's situation for one factor
2 marks: Identifies two factors contributing to youth unemployment with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about youth employment
markerNotes: Name three distinct factors and give a brief explanation of each one.
Use the scenario to illustrate one factor, such as transport and location limiting access to jobs.
Factors that overlap, such as two forms of lack of experience, count only once.
commonStudentErrors: Listing causes of unemployment in general without connecting them to youth employment.
Stating a factor without any explanation of how it contributes to unemployment.
Using the scenario only as a description without linking it to a factor.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this case study, several factors contributing to youth unemployment can be identified. First, many young people have limited work experience, which employers often value when choosing between applicants. Second, the number of entry-level positions in a local area may be small, so competition for them is strong. Third, transport and location can limit access to jobs. For Lachlan, the lack of local employers he can reach by public transport means he must rely on a small number of options when applying for his apprenticeship, which shows how youth employment can be limited by location.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines three distinct factors, each briefly explained, and illustrates one with the scenario. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Young people may have little work experience. Transport can make it hard to reach jobs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two factors with limited detail and no link to Lachlan. This is the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss how paid work can support young people to manage multiple roles, and explain how Amara could optimise her employment prospects.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Amara is 22, a university student in Sydney who works 18 hours a week as a barista. She helps her younger brother with homework after school and is a volunteer tutor with a community program.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses in detail how paid work supports young people to manage multiple roles and how Amara could optimise her employment prospects, with clear links to the case study
5 marks: Discusses how paid work supports young people to manage multiple roles, with clear links to Amara's situation
4 marks: Explains how paid work can help a young person manage multiple roles, with some links to the scenario
3 marks: Describes some ways paid work affects young people's roles, with limited links to Amara
2 marks: Identifies a role Amara holds with a limited link to paid work
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about youth employment
markerNotes: Discuss both the support paid work gives and its limits for Amara, then turn to the steps she could take.
Use the scenario details, such as the 18-hour roster and homework help, to show the trade-offs.
Credit transferable skills, such as communication and teamwork, as a way to improve employment prospects.
commonStudentErrors: Describing paid work in general without discussing how it supports young people's multiple roles.
Answering only the discussion part and omitting how Amara could optimise her employment prospects.
Suggesting employment strategies that do not relate to Amara's roles or skills.

sampleAnswers.answer: This case study of youth employment shows that paid work can support young people to manage multiple roles when it is flexible and suits their other commitments. Amara's work as a barista gives her income for university and some independence, and her roster keeps her study times free. However, 18 hours a week is demanding, and it can limit the time she has to help her brother with homework. To optimise her employment prospects, Amara could build transferable skills for hospitality management or customer service, such as communication, teamwork and time management. She could also seek work with more predictable hours, which would let her keep her tutoring and family responsibilities. In this way, paid work can help a young person balance roles, provided it is structured around them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the support and limits of paid work for Amara and sets out steps to optimise her prospects, with clear links to the case study. This meets the top row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Paid work can help young people manage multiple roles because it gives them income and a routine. Amara's barista shifts pay for her study, but the hours may clash with her brother's needs. She could improve her employment prospects by building teamwork and communication skills.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how paid work supports Amara with some links to the scenario, but the discussion of limits and the steps are brief. This is the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Amara works as a barista and studies at university. Her job gives her some money.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a role with a limited link to paid work and no discussion. This is the 2-mark row.
